a_rows_sample.anchor:
The central distinction is: Supported 
eq Accepted 
eq Committed 
eq True. This distinction should become one of the core laws of KnowledgeOS.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the governing distinction of Step 8 as a candidate core law of KnowledgeOS: Supported ≠ Accepted ≠ Committed ≠ True.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The problem ... Strong supporting evidence, No known contradiction, Current, High provenance quality ... Can KnowledgeOS now put P into the Knowledge State as accepted knowledge? Not necessarily. There is a missing concept: AcceptancePolicy. The evidence tells us what the evidence supports. The acce
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues even strong, uncontradicted, current, high-provenance evidence does not automatically warrant acceptance, introducing AcceptancePolicy as the missing concept determining what may be admitted as accepted knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Four epistemic statuses ... Candidate \rightarrow Supported \rightarrow Accepted \rightarrow Committed ... Supported \rightarrow Contested ... Supported \rightarrow Rejected ... Candidate \rightarrow Unresolved ... These are not simply levels of "confidence." They represent different domain states.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Candidate/Supported/Accepted/Committed as a branching progression (not a confidence scale), with additional branches to Contested, Rejected, and Unresolved, insisting these are distinct domain states.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate ... A proposition becomes a candidate when KnowledgeOS has reason to represent it but does not yet have sufficient basis to accept it. ... LLM extracted from document ... Candidate(P)=True but Accepted(P)=False. This is particularly important for AI-generated knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Candidate(P) status (proposition represented but not yet accepted), illustrated by an LLM-extracted proposition, flagged as particularly important for AI-generated knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Supported ... Supported_\rho(P) = Assessment_\rho(P)\models SupportCondition_\rho ... The evidence provides a defensible basis for the proposition under the selected assessment policy. But Supported(P)\not\Rightarrow Accepted(P).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Supported_ρ(P) as Assessment_ρ(P) satisfying a policy-specific SupportCondition_ρ, explicitly not implying Accepted(P).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Accepted ... Accept_\rho(P,EA) \rightarrow AcceptedAssertion subject to the acceptance policy. ... One authoritative current source is sufficient ... Two independent observations ... Accepted_{\rho_1}(P)=True while Accepted_{\rho_2}(P)=False. This is not a mathematical contradiction. It is policy de
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Accept_ρ(P,EA)→AcceptedAssertion as policy-relative, showing the same evidence can be Accepted under one policy (single authoritative source) and not under another (requiring two independent observations) — policy dependence, not contradiction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Commitment ... an organization may accept ... but still not be committed to using that assertion as a basis for an operational decision. "We accept that Nexus is 3.69, but migration approval requires an additional infrastructure verification." Accepted(P)\not\Rightarrow Committed(P). Commitment mean
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Commitment as distinct from Acceptance: Accepted(P) ⇏ Committed(P), illustrated by an organization accepting a fact but still requiring additional verification before migration approval; commitment means willingness to rely on the proposition for a defined purpose/action.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Commitment is purpose-dependent ... Commit_\rho(P,Purpose,Authority) ... Commit(P,migration,ArchitectureBoard) may require more than Commit(P,internal research,Engineer). Commit(P,P_1)\neq Commit(P,P_2). This fits our earlier Ideal State principle: I_t(P_1)\neq I_t(P_2).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Commit_ρ(P,Purpose,Authority) as purpose-dependent, e.g. migration commitment requiring Architecture Board authority versus lighter requirements for internal research, echoing the earlier purpose-dependence of the Ideal State.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Truth remains outside the state machine ... Accepted(P)\neq True(P) and Committed(P)\neq True(P). KnowledgeOS does not have an oracle for reality. It records what is currently supported, accepted, and/or committed under a defined epistemic and governance regime.
a_rows_sample.statement: States that neither Accepted(P) nor Committed(P) equals True(P): KnowledgeOS has no oracle for reality, only records what is supported/accepted/committed under a defined regime.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Formal acceptance function ... \alpha_\rho: EA\times P\times C \rightarrow \mathcal S_A ... \mathcal S_A=\{Candidate,Supported,Accepted,Rejected,Contested,Unresolved\} ... an assertion can be Supported + Contested. So again, we should be careful about a single enum.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines α_ρ:EA×P×C→S_A over six statuses, warning against treating S_A as a single mutually-exclusive enum since e.g. Supported+Contested can co-occur.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Better: acceptance as a multidimensional status ... \Omega_A=(SupportStatus,AcceptanceStatus,CommitmentStatus,ContestStatus) ... Support: Strong, Acceptance: Accepted, Commitment: Committed, Contest: Active. This looks strange initially, but it accurately represents real organizational knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines acceptance status as a four-dimensional vector Ω_A=(SupportStatus,AcceptanceStatus,CommitmentStatus,ContestStatus), with a worked example showing Accepted+Committed+Contest:Active as coherent, accurately reflecting real organizational knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Why "Accepted + Contested" is possible ... an architecture board has formally accepted ... another architect disputes ... Accepted(P)=True while Contested(P)=True. This is not logically impossible. ... The proposition is institutionally accepted while still being epistemically contested. This is exa
a_rows_sample.statement: Justifies Accepted+Contested coexisting via an architecture-board example (formally accepted decision still disputed by an architect), establishing that epistemic status and governance status must not be collapsed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Acceptance policy ... \rho_A = AcceptancePolicy ... Evidence requirements N_{independent}\geq2 ... Source requirements Authority(Source)\geq A_{min} ... Temporal requirements Age(e)\leq T_{max} ... Conflict requirements ActiveConflict(P)=False ... Human approval ... Statistical threshold Pr(P\mid E)
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines AcceptancePolicy ρ_A as specifying six example condition types (independent-evidence count, source authority minimum, evidence-age maximum, no active conflict, human approval, statistical threshold) — explicitly examples of policy, not universal law.

a_rows_sample.anchor: This gives us a clean separation ... Mathematics defines what the evidence assessment means. Policy defines when an assessment is sufficient for acceptance. Governance defines who has authority to commit to that knowledge. Assessment \rightarrow AcceptancePolicy \rightarrow Acceptance \rightarrow Go
a_rows_sample.statement: Draws a three-way separation — mathematics (what assessment means), policy (when acceptance is sufficient), governance (who may commit) — formalized as Assessment→AcceptancePolicy→Acceptance→Governance→Commitment.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DDD interpretation ... a bounded context around Knowledge Commitment. Assertion ... EvidenceAssessment ... AcceptancePolicy ... AcceptanceDecision ... Commitment ... Authority ... These should not be hidden inside the Assertion entity.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a Knowledge Commitment bounded context with six concepts (Assertion, EvidenceAssessment, AcceptancePolicy, AcceptanceDecision, Commitment, Authority) that must not be hidden inside the Assertion entity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Acceptance is a domain event ... AssertionAccepted should be emitted. AssertionId, AssessmentId, PolicyId, PolicyVersion, Authority, Context, EffectiveFrom, DecisionBasis, Timestamp. This creates an auditable transition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines an AssertionAccepted domain event carrying AssertionId, AssessmentId, PolicyId/Version, Authority, Context, EffectiveFrom, DecisionBasis, Timestamp for auditability.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Rejection is different from absence of acceptance ... NotAccepted\neq Rejected ... Evidence: insufficient ... The correct state may be Unresolved. It does not mean P=False. Unresolved\neq Rejected. This is critical for incomplete real-world knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: States NotAccepted≠Rejected and Unresolved≠Rejected: insufficient evidence should yield Unresolved, not a claim that P is false — critical for incomplete real-world knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Example ... Production Nexus is backed up. ... Infrastructure engineer says yes ... Backup configuration not inspected ... No restore test ... Support: Moderate, Uncertainty: High, Verification: Insufficient ... KnowledgeOS should not conclude \neg P. Nor Accepted(P). The correct result may be Unres
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a backup-verification example where weak/unverified evidence (engineer's verbal yes, uninspected config, no restore test) correctly yields Unresolved(P) with a Lord recommendation to verify configuration and run a restore test, rather than either Accepted(P) or ¬P.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Acceptance and Ideal State ... MustBeVerified(BackupStatus) ... Supported(P) may still fail the ideal requirement: \Sigma_K(P)\not\models I^K(P). Accepted(P) \not\Rightarrow IdealSatisfied(P). A proposition can be accepted while the knowledge objective remains incomplete.
a_rows_sample.statement: Connects Acceptance to the Ideal State: Accepted(P) ⇏ IdealSatisfied(P) — a proposition can be accepted while the underlying knowledge objective (e.g. independent verification) remains incomplete.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Example ... Nexus = 3.69 Accepted. But the Ideal State requires MustBeKnown, MustBeCurrent, MustBeIndependentlyVerified ... Independent verification = no ... Accepted(P)=True but \Delta_t\neq\emptyset. Acceptance does not mean completion.
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: an accepted Nexus-version assertion still leaves a nonempty discrepancy Δ_t because independent verification is missing — 'Acceptance does not mean completion.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: The fundamental problem ... P\land\neg P ... principle of explosion ... P,\neg P\vdash Q for arbitrary Q, the Knowledge State becomes useless. KnowledgeOS must tolerate contradiction without logical explosion.
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires KnowledgeOS tolerate contradiction (P∧¬P) without classical logical explosion (P,¬P⊢Q for arbitrary Q), since explosion would make the Knowledge State useless.

b_rows_sample.anchor: First distinction: contradiction versus inconsistency ... Contradiction ... Conflict(A_1,A_2,Ctx)=True. Inconsistency ... a set of assertions that cannot all simultaneously satisfy a specified logical model. Contradiction is relational. Inconsistency is a property of a set/state.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Contradiction (a relational property between two specific assertions under a context) from Inconsistency (a property of an entire assertion set/state under a logical model).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Context must be checked first ... Nexus_{Production}=3.70 and Nexus_{Staging}=3.69 ... no contradiction because Context(P_1)\neq Context(P_2). Different context \Rightarrow not necessarily contradictory. Many apparent contradictions are actually missing-dimension problems.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms that differing contexts (production vs staging) can make apparently conflicting values non-contradictory, restating that many apparent contradictions are missing-dimension problems.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Contradiction requires a conflict rule ... Conflict_\rho(A_i,A_j) = Rule_\rho(P_i,P_j,C_i,C_j) ... Version(x)=v_1 \land Version(x)=v_2 \land v_1\neq v_2 is contradictory if the two assertions refer to the same system; same environment; same temporal scope. Without those conditions: DifferentValues\n
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Conflict_ρ(A_i,A_j)=Rule_ρ(P_i,P_j,C_i,C_j): contradiction requires an explicit rule checking same system/environment/temporal scope, so DifferentValues ≠ Contradiction without those conditions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Conflict graph ... a knowledge conflict graph: G_C=(A,L_C) ... A1: Nexus production = 3.69 conflict A2: Nexus production = 3.70. The conflict is explicitly represented. Neither assertion has to be deleted.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a knowledge conflict graph G_C=(A,L_C) (assertions and conflict relations) representing conflicts explicitly without deleting either assertion.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS should preserve both assertions ... A_1\in K_t \land A_2\in K_t \land Conflict(A_1,A_2)=Active. This is a legitimate Knowledge State. The state is inconsistent with respect to that proposition, but it is not computationally unusable.
b_rows_sample.statement: States that a Knowledge State holding both A1 and A2 with an Active conflict marker is legitimate and computationally usable, despite being inconsistent with respect to that proposition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Paraconsistent principle ... P,\neg P \not\Rightarrow Q for arbitrary Q. Contradiction must remain local. ... we do not necessarily need to commit the entire KnowledgeOS kernel to one particular paraconsistent logic ... the kernel must support the invariant: Local inconsistency does not imply global
b_rows_sample.statement: States the paraconsistent principle P,¬P ⇏ Q (contradiction must remain local), without committing the kernel to any specific paraconsistent logic (e.g. Priest's LP), requiring only that local inconsistency not imply global triviality.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A useful four-valued interpretation ... P supported ... \neg P supported ... Unknown ... Supported true-side ... Supported false-side ... Conflicted ... \mathbb B=\{00,10,01,11\} ... This is much more expressive than True/False.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a four-valued epistemic-status model B={00,10,01,11} (Unknown, P-supported, ¬P-supported, Conflicted) as more expressive than binary True/False.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Important correction ... We should not interpret 10=True and 01=False. They mean: Evidence currently supports one side. This is epistemic status, not metaphysical truth. Four-valued epistemic status\neq Four-valued truth.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects a likely misreading of the four-valued model: its values denote epistemic support status, not metaphysical truth values — Four-valued epistemic status ≠ Four-valued truth.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This fits our existing epistemic model ... \Sigma_A=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) and conflict remains external: C=(A_i,A_j,Rule,Context,Status). \Sigma_A does not need to contain Conflicted because conflict belongs to the relationship between assertions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Confirms conflict is a relational property external to the per-assertion state Σ_A, which need not include a 'Conflicted' field since conflict belongs between assertions, not within one.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Conflict intensity is not a universal scalar ... ConflictScore=0.8 ... I recommend we don't. Instead represent Conflict: Assertions, Rule, Context, EvidenceBasis, Status: Active. Conflict representation is fundamental. Conflict score is derived.
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns against a scalar ConflictScore, preferring a structured conflict record (assertions, rule, context, evidence basis, status): conflict representation is fundamental, any scalar score is derived.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Belief revision ... K_t\models P and new evidence supports \neg P. K_{t+1}=Revise(K_t,e). Revision does not necessarily mean deleting P. retain both and mark conflict; contextualize; downgrade one; retract one; supersede one; accept one and reject the other; leave unresolved. Which occurs depends on
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the revision operation K_{t+1}=Revise(K_t,e) with seven possible policy-dependent outcomes (retain both with conflict marked, contextualize, downgrade, retract, supersede, accept-one-reject-other, leave unresolved) — none of which is automatic deletion.

b_rows_sample.anchor: AGM-style belief revision is useful—but not sufficient ... revision; contraction; consistency; minimal change. But KnowledgeOS has a different requirement: We may intentionally retain inconsistent information. Therefore classical consistency-preserving belief revision is not sufficient as the sole k
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues classical AGM-style (consistency-preserving) belief revision is insufficient alone, since KnowledgeOS may intentionally retain inconsistent information; needs a more general evidence-based, contradiction-tolerant revision model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Three different responses to conflict ... A. Contextual resolution ... No real contradiction. B. Epistemic resolution ... one assertion may become Retracted or Rejected. C. Irreducible conflict ... Conflict=Unresolved and KnowledgeOS retains both. This is a perfectly legitimate endpoint.
b_rows_sample.statement: Classifies three conflict responses: Contextual resolution (no real contradiction once context is added), Epistemic resolution (one side retracted/rejected on evidential grounds), and Irreducible conflict (both retained as Unresolved, a legitimate endpoint).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Unresolvable is not failure ... two authoritative sources disagree and there is no way to determine which is correct. KnowledgeOS should be able to say P: Contested rather than inventing P=True. Unresolvable is a valid knowledge state.
b_rows_sample.statement: States Unresolvable is a valid knowledge state: when two authoritative sources irreconcilably disagree, KnowledgeOS should record P:Contested rather than inventing a resolution.

b_rows_sample.anchor: What should Zero do? ... Zero detects Conflict(A_1,A_2). It creates a discrepancy d_{conflict} with involved assertions; conflict rule; context; severity; evidence basis; age; impact. Zero(K,I) \rightarrow \Delta_{conflict}.
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends Zero's role to conflict detection: Zero(K,I)→Δ_conflict, a structured discrepancy record with assertions, rule, context, severity, evidence basis, age, impact.

b_rows_sample.anchor: What should Lord do? ... What information could resolve this conflict? ... Query live API. Inspect deployment manifest. Inspect filesystem. Ask system owner. The candidates are evaluated using Step 6: VOE(q). Conflict \rightarrow Gap \rightarrow CandidateEvidence \rightarrow ExpectedDiscrepancyReduc
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends Lord's role to conflict resolution: proposing candidate evidence acquisitions (query API, inspect manifest/filesystem, ask owner) evaluated via the Step 6 Value-of-Evidence machinery, connecting Conflict→Gap→CandidateEvidence→ExpectedDiscrepancyReduction.

b_rows_sample.anchor: What should Sārathi do? ... severity; purpose; cost; authority; safety; urgency; expected value. It may decide Investigate. Or AcceptRisk. Or Defer. Or CommitWithConflict. A decision does not necessarily require complete epistemic resolution.
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends Sārathi's role to conflict handling with four possible decisions (Investigate/AcceptRisk/Defer/CommitWithConflict), noting a decision does not require complete epistemic resolution.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Example — Architecture decision ... Migration is technically feasible ... Migration introduces unacceptable operational risk ... TechnicalFeasibility=True ... OperationalRisk=High ... the apparent conflict becomes a multi-dimensional decision problem. Conflict detection can reveal a modeling deficie
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows an apparent architecture-decision contradiction (feasible vs unacceptable risk) resolves into a multi-dimensional decision problem once separated into distinct dimensions (TechnicalFeasibility, OperationalRisk) — conflict detection can reveal a modeling deficiency.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Temporal conflict ... Nexus=3.69 at t_1=2024 and Nexus=3.85 at t_2=2026. There is no contradiction if t_1\neq t_2. Temporal context must be part of conflict detection. This is one of the reasons we separated SourceTime, AcquisitionTime, ValidityTime.
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires temporal context be part of conflict detection, since two differently-timed version assertions are not contradictory — reaffirming the earlier SourceTime/AcquisitionTime/ValidityTime separation.

b_aliases: Step 9: Contradiction, Paraconsistency, and Belief Revision

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'paraconsistent-belief-revision' POSSIBLY relates to 'epistemic-acceptance-commitment' (batch B0021). Note: S0864's Step 9: distinguishes Contradiction (relational) from Inconsistency (state property), defines a knowledge conflict graph, a four-valued epistemic-status model, a nine-operation belief-revision set, minimal-revision and dependency-propagation-as-reassessment principles, kernel-decidability vs open-world semantic inference, and C1-C8 invariants guaranteeing contradiction tolerance without logical explosion; hands off to Step 10 (inference and derivation).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Independent epistemic anchors; real independence (Human->SourceEvidence, not AI->Human)
a_rows_sample.statement: To prevent epistemic self-sealing, defines potential anchors: ExternalEvidence, HumanReview, IndependentTest, GroundTruth, ControlledExperiment -- but independence must be real: HumanReview of only the AI's conclusion (AI->Human) creates dependency, whereas Human->SourceEvidence independently is a stronger anchor. Defines Anchor(A) as evidence/validation whose epistemic generation is sufficiently independent of the system's current belief/policy, to be operationalized per domain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Anchor diversity, common-mode epistemic failure, and epistemic redundancy != number of opinions
a_rows_sample.statement: Since one anchor may itself be wrong, high-criticality knowledge should use an AnchorSet={A1,...,An} whose members must not share the same hidden source -- if A1,A2,A3 all derive from the same database they are not three independent confirmations ('common-mode failure' analog for epistemics). True redundancy requires diversity of source, method, model, measurement, and reasoning path, so EpistemicRedundancy != NumberOfOpinions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Champion/challenger adversarial review and a falsification budget
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends champion/challenger to epistemic control: an independent M_challenger should ideally use different assumptions, independent evidence, and different methodology; the challenger asks 'what would falsify the current conclusion' rather than 'can I support it', creating FalsificationPressure. Proposes a deliberate Budget_falsification: for critical decisions, resources should be reserved specifically to try disproving the preferred hypothesis, since a system optimized only for DecisionSuccess may stop searching once it finds supporting evidence, while one optimized partly for Falsification actively searches for failure modes.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Safe learning architecture diagram: Support and Falsify must coexist
a_rows_sample.statement: Depicts a safe-learning pipeline: Experience -> Evaluation -> Learning Candidate -> {Support, Falsify} -> Validation -> Independent Check -> Promotion -> New Knowledge, with the key point that Support and Falsify must coexist as parallel branches feeding validation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Reality-based evaluation: RealityGap_t = Distance(Prediction_t, Observation_t); no-self-certification principle
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the strongest anchor against self-deception as Reality: KnowledgeOS must periodically compare ModelPrediction against ObservedWorldOutcome, formalized as RealityGap_t = Distance(Prediction_t, Observation_t), with repeated RealityGap growth triggering investigation. States one of Step 47's strongest principles: KnowledgeOS must not be the sole authority for validating its own critical knowledge -- for critical knowledge an external or independent validation path should exist, though independence need not mean humans everywhere (another measurement system, independent test, formal proof, external source, controlled experiment, or a separately designed model all qualify).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Twelve falsification experiments for Step 47 epistemic-control model (all PASS)
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs twelve falsification tests, all PASS: (1) KnowledgeOS strengthens a belief using evidence generated by its own previous policy => evidence dependency recognized; (2) the system converges on a stable but incorrect model => stability not interpreted as correctness; (3) a challenger model contradicts the champion => disagreement preserved and investigated; (4) new evidence reduces confidence => confidence can decrease; (5) a trusted claim becomes invalid => demoted without deleting its history; (6) an AI-generated hypothesis has no independent evidence => cannot automatically become operational knowledge; (7) a candidate learning policy would improve information gain but violate a safety constraint => safety blocks the exploration; (8) a model update improves average accuracy but violates a critical invariant => promotion rejected; (9) multiple validation results share the same underlying source => not counted as independent confirmation; (10) a historical interpretation is later disproven => historical decision remains reproducible using its original knowledge state; (11) the system's own policy changes the population from which evidence is collected => policy-induced distribution shift represented; (12) the model becomes increasingly confident while prediction error simultaneously increases => calibration/reality-gap mechanism flags epistemic instability or model failure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Step 47 verdict and seven core principles of epistemic control
a_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 47 -- PASS ('a formal foundation for epistemic control... the system must be able to determine whether its own learning process remains trustworthy') and restates seven core principles: self-generated evidence is not automatically independent evidence; stable knowledge is not necessarily correct knowledge; confidence must be allowed to decrease; critical knowledge requires independent epistemic anchors; learning must be governed; falsification must be a first-class operation; KnowledgeOS may learn from outcomes but must not use its own conclusions as unquestionable proof of those conclusions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Non-circular calibration: an AI must not validate itself using only its own generated outcomes (another epistemic firewall)
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns an AI model must not determine its own calibration using only its own generated outcomes -- externally grounded outcomes are needed, else AI -> AI evaluation -> AI confidence becomes circular; prefers Prediction -> ExternalOutcome -> Evaluation, described as 'another epistemic firewall'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Self-certification rejected as circular validation; DifferentModel⇏IndependentEvidence; model dependency graph G_M
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies the self-validation problem: Model_A evaluating Model_A with the same assumptions/outputs creates circular validation (A->A). Experiment 6: an AI asserting its own prediction is reliable with no independent outcome yields NotValidated -- PASS. Prefers Prediction -> ExternalOutcome -> Evaluation (evaluator: separate model, deterministic rules, measured outcome, human assessment, or independent statistical process). Warns two models trained on the same data sharing the same failure mechanism are not necessarily independent validators: DifferentModel ⇏ IndependentEvidence. Experiment 7: Model_B evaluating Model_A using the same generated predictions without independent outcomes yields validation strength not equivalent to independent validation -- PASS. Extends the provenance graph to a model dependency graph G_M=(Models,Dependencies) (M_A -> M_B if M_B's evaluation depends on M_A's outputs), preventing false claims of independent validation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Provenance != AuthenticProvenance; six concepts requiring separation (Identity/Authenticity/Integrity/Authority/Trust/Provenance)
b_rows_sample.statement: States provenance can be falsified: Provenance != AuthenticProvenance. Separates six related-but-distinct concepts: Identity ('who or what is this?' -- proves nothing about truth; experiment 1 rejects inferring p=True merely because an identity is valid and asserted p); Authenticity ('did this artifact actually originate from the claimed identity?', VerifySignature(a,Agent_A)->True/False); Integrity ('has the artifact changed since creation/signing?', a hash H(a) changing to H(a') on modification -- experiment 2 detects IntegrityViolation, and Integrity != Truth, experiment 3 shows a validly-signed false claim gives Authentic=True but TruthStatus=Conflicted, 'cryptography protects provenance and integrity; it does not manufacture truth'); Authority ('is this identity authorized to make this statement/decision?', context-scoped -- experiment 4 rejects an authority overreach from TechnicalAnalysis into FinancialAuthorization); Trust (Trust(x,y,C,t), contextual and non-transferable across domains -- experiment 5 rejects transferring code-analysis reliability into financial-decision authority); and Provenance itself.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Reliability != Trust; sk/pk signature model with key compromise/revocation and temporal IdentityValidityAtTime
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes empirically-estimable Reliability(A,C) = correct/evaluated outcomes from Trust, which may additionally incorporate authority, security, provenance, policy, and historical behavior -- experiment 6: 99% accuracy with a compromised identity does not automatically give Trust=99%. Introduces asymmetric cryptographic identity (sk,pk), signing sigma=Sign_sk(H(a)), verification Verify_pk(a,sigma); experiment 7 accepts AuthenticOrigin=A given valid verification (subject to key-management assumptions). Notes CryptographicTrust depends on KeyManagement: experiment 8 shows a compromised sk_A producing technically-valid signatures for forged content a', requiring the system to consider key revocation/status. Gives identity a lifecycle (Active/Suspended/Revoked/Expired) and requires IdentityValidityAtTime: experiment 9 confirms a signature made before revocation (SignTime<t_revocation) remains HistoricalSignatureValid subject to the trust model, connecting to temporal epistemics (TruthAtTime and IdentityValidityAtTime both required, so Trust must potentially be time-indexed).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Cryptographic provenance chain with hash-linked transformations; broken/forged-edge detection; Merkle tamper evidence; no-blockchain-required principle
b_rows_sample.statement: Constructs a cryptographic provenance chain A0 --Sign--> A1 --Transform--> A2 --Sign--> A3, each transformation recording InputHash, OutputHash, ActorIdentity, TransformationVersion. Experiment 10: A2 claiming derivation from A1 but with a mismatched recorded input hash yields ProvenanceIntegrityViolation -- PASS. Extends this to a graph G=(V,E) with cryptographically-bearing edges (Actor, Timestamp, Transformation, InputHash, OutputHash); experiment 11: an attacker forging DerivedFrom(A3,A2) into DerivedFrom(A3,A9) yields GraphIntegrityViolation given protected provenance records -- PASS. Introduces Merkle-style hash trees (H_root=H(H_1,...,H_n)) for large provenance structures, letting a verifier check membership without storing every verification result independently. States explicitly: the architectural requirement is TamperEvidence, not Blockchain -- 'we do not need blockchain... a cryptographically verifiable append-only event history can be implemented with conventional infrastructure'. Experiment 12: replacing ordinary append-only storage with blockchain solely because 'knowledge must be trustworthy' yields NotRequired -- 'trust properties must be derived from actual requirements'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Authenticity is orthogonal to truth (restated); AuthenticEvidence != ReliableEvidence; four/five-layer trust model
b_rows_sample.statement: Restates: Sign_A(p)=Valid tells us only that A authored/signed p, not that p=True -- Authenticity is orthogonal to truth. Experiment 13: a validly signed 'the server is healthy' with no actual server evidence yields AuthenticatedClaim, not VerifiedSystemState -- PASS. Gives a five-layer trust model: Layer 1 Identity (who?), Layer 2 Authenticity (did they produce it?), Layer 3 Integrity (was it modified?), Layer 4 Epistemic validity (does evidence justify the claim?), Layer 5 Authority (are they permitted to perform this operation?). Later reinforces with the principle AuthenticEvidence != ReliableEvidence (someone can honestly and authentically provide bad information) -- experiment 22: internally consistent, cryptographically authentic evidence from a historically unreliable source yields Authentic=True but EvidenceStrength not automatically high -- PASS; and ReliableSource != CorrectEveryTime (statistics remain probabilistic, uncertainty must be preserved).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Unified TrustAssessment function rejects a single trusted=true flag; God-Object TrustObject FAILs
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines TrustAssessment(a) = f(Identity, Authenticity, Integrity, Authority, EpistemicSupport, Context, Time) -- 'no single Boolean can represent all of this safely'. Experiment 14: storing a bare trusted=true for an artifact with valid identity/integrity but absent authority and weak evidence is Rejected as an insufficient trust representation -- PASS. Warns against one enormous Trust aggregate, recommending separate concepts (Identity, Credential, Authority, EvidenceAssessment, Provenance) with explicit relationships, potentially separate bounded contexts (IdentityContext, EvidenceContext, KnowledgeContext, GovernanceContext) integrated via contracts. Experiment 15: a universal TrustObject bundling identity/authorization/reliability/truth/evidence/risk/reputation yields GodObjectRisk -- explicitly FAIL.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Capability-based authorization for humans and AI; delegation-scope violation; least privilege Capability(A)⊆RequiredCapabilities(A)
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces delegated authority chains (A delegates to B, B may authorize only within its delegated scope); experiment 16: B granting C a scope S1∪S2 it never possessed (only S1) yields DelegationViolation -- PASS. Defines typed Capability=(Subject,Action,Resource,Scope,Validity), stronger than role-only authorization; experiment 17: an agent with Capability(Action=X) attempting Action=Y is Denied -- PASS. Applies the same model to humans: Person != UniversalAuthority (architecture-approval authority does not imply deployment authority) -- experiment 18: role overreach interpreted as deployment authority is Denied -- PASS. Applies it to AI agents with a bounded CapabilitySet (e.g. ReadKnowledge, CreateHypothesis, RunAnalysis, but not AuthorizePayment or DeleteEvidence) -- experiment 19: an unrestricted AI agent receiving full system privileges is a GovernanceFailure -- PASS. States the least-privilege principle Capability(A) subset-of RequiredCapabilities(A), aligning security architecture with DDD responsibility boundaries.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Trust non-transitivity; multi-graph model (G_K,G_P,G_D,G_A,G_T) not collapsible (generic-relation-schema FAILs)
b_rows_sample.statement: States trust transitivity is not universally valid: Trust(A,B)=High and Trust(B,C)=High does not license Trust(A,C)=High -- experiment 20 rejects that inference -- PASS, 'prevents dangerous trust propagation through agent networks'. Extends the multi-graph family with a Trust graph G_T alongside Knowledge (G_K), Provenance (G_P), Dependency (G_D), and Authority (G_A) graphs, which 'should not be collapsed into one universal graph'. Experiment 21: representing all relationships as one generic relation(source,target,type) with no bounded semantics yields SemanticAmbiguity -- explicitly FAIL, 'the relationships have different invariants' -- while noting a higher-level system may still correlate G_K/G_P/G_A while each retains its own domain semantics.

b_rows_sample.anchor: VerifiableEpistemicProvenance (cryptographic + epistemic provenance combined); SemanticTrustBoundary between unverified input and trusted state
b_rows_sample.statement: Combines Epistemic provenance ('why do we believe this?') with Cryptographic provenance ('can we verify the recorded history?') into VerifiableEpistemicProvenance -- 'a major architectural concept'. Defines a SemanticTrustBoundary between UnverifiedInput and TrustedKnowledgeState: no artifact crosses merely because an AI generated it. Experiment 23: an AI-generated claim with identity, signature, and provenance but no supporting evidence yields AuthenticatedClaim, but NotVerifiedKnowledge -- PASS, 'perhaps the most important distinction of Step 73': a secure AI platform must not confuse 'who said this' with 'why should we believe this'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Kernel updated to add Identity: K_OS=Artifact+Type+Identity+Provenance+Event+Invariant+Transformation+Policy
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues Identity should now be considered a kernel-level concern (trustworthy provenance requires attribution), while cryptographic implementation (PKI/HSM/KeyVault) remains infrastructure, not kernel-native. Updates the kernel to K_OS = Artifact + Type + Identity + Provenance + Event + Invariant + Transformation + Policy, with State as the operational projection.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 73 verdict: trustworthy provenance = Identity+Authenticity+Integrity+EpistemicProvenance+Context+Authority; opens Step 74 (already covered)
b_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 73 -- PASS: trustworthy provenance = Identity + Authenticity + Integrity + Epistemic provenance + Context + Authority -- never merely a hash, a signature, or AI confidence. Summarizes the pipeline Reality -> Observation -> Measurement -> Evidence -> Typed Inference -> Knowledge -> Decision -> Authorization -> Action -> Outcome, with every meaningful transition carrying Identity + Provenance + Version + Invariant + Policy + TrustMetadata, and explicit handling of Uncertainty, Contradiction, Concurrency, PartialObservability, ComputationalLimits, Authority, Trust. Opens Step 74 (causal knowledge of decisions and outcomes, already covered as S0972): distinguishing TemporalOrder, Dependency, CausalInfluence, Intervention, and CounterfactualEffect since merely observing a decision before an outcome does not establish that the decision caused it.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Agent communication requires a governed Message->CandidateArtifact->ValidatedArtifact pipeline; peer assertions are not automatically knowledge (Experiment 24); context-specific inter-agent trust and reputation must yield to fresh evidence (Experiments 25-26)
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires agent communication (Messages or Artifacts) to pass through Message -> CandidateArtifact -> ValidatedArtifact rather than becoming knowledge directly. Experiment 24: Agent A tells Agent B 'the production database is healthy' and B immediately records DatabaseHealthy=True -- expected Rejected unless the communication protocol explicitly treats A's statement as authoritative evidence -- PASS. Revisits Step 73's trust model to require context-specific trust: Trust(B,A,Architecture) may differ from Trust(B,A,Operations). Experiment 25: Agent B treats A's high architecture reliability as equally reliable for production-incident statements -- expected UnsupportedTrustTransfer -- PASS. Introduces reputation Reliability(A,C,t) from historical performance, which must never override direct evidence where stronger evidence exists. Experiment 26: agent reputation 99% but fresh evidence contradicts the agent -- expected fresh evidence must be considered -- PASS.

b_aliases: Step 73 Identity, Trust and Cryptographic Provenance

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'kos-identity-trust-cryptographic-provenance' POSSIBLY relates to 'epistemic-anchor-redundancy-model' (batch B0023). Note: Step 73's identity/trust/cryptographic-provenance layer: the six-concept separation (Identity/Authenticity/Integrity/Authority/Trust/Provenance), signature/key-revocation/temporal-validity, Merkle tamper evidence with an explicit no-blockchain-required principle, the unified multi-dimensional TrustAssessment function, capability-based least-privilege authorization for humans and AI, trust non-transitivity, the multi-graph non-collapse requirement extended with a Trust graph G_T, and VerifiableEpistemicProvenance/SemanticTrustBoundary. Complements epistemic-anchor-redundancy-model (Step 47, which addresses independence of validation sources) with the cryptographic/identity dimension of trust.

a_rows_sample.anchor:
each iteration introduces additional difficulty; knowledge operators do not automatically iterate. ... K(p)
ot\Rightarrow K(K(p)) ... K^n(p)
ot\Rightarrow K^{n+1}(p) ... Verified(x)\Rightarrow Verified(Verification(x)) [dangerous hidden assumption] ... Verification 
eq MetaVerification
a_rows_sample.statement: Epistemic Iteration Non-Closure: K^n(p) does not imply K^{n+1}(p) unless a separate rule/evidence/authority establishes the higher-order knowledge, guarding against 'the system knows X therefore it knows that it knows X'; applied to the Determination->Decision->Action->Observation->Verification chain to reject the hidden assumption Verified(x)=>Verified(Verification(x)), giving Verification != MetaVerification (Verify(V) requires its own evidence/context/authority). Status: [DERIVED].

a_rows_sample.anchor: EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING ... EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED] ... EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP — strong research candidate] ... EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP]
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes an 8-section theory addition 'EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING': EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED], EL.2 Epistemic Non-Transparency [DERIVED], EL.3 Knowledge Iteration [DERIVED], EL.4 Evidence Relativity [PROP], EL.5 Margin of Error [PROP], EL.6 Accessibility (distinguishing Truth/Knowability/Accessibility/ActualKnowledge) [DERIVED], EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP-strong], EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP], consolidating this file's individual candidates into one proposed section.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Mr Magoo sees a tree ... he cannot know for any i that the tree is not i inches tall ... Therefore, KK (knowledge that one knows) fails. ... Further iterations of knowledge are even harder to achieve.
a_rows_sample.statement: The Mr-Magoo margin-for-error argument formally derives the failure of the KK principle (knowledge does not imply knowledge of knowledge) via a step-by-step discrimination-limit argument, and notes iterations beyond the second are progressively harder to achieve -- the original formal source for the epistemic-iteration-non-closure principle.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What to Adopt: Knowledge First ✅ ... Evidence = Knowledge ✅ ... Factive Mental States ✅ ... Non-Luminosity ✅ ... Margin for Error ✅ ... Anti-KK ✅ ... Knowledge Rule for Assertion ✅ ... What to Reject: Knowledge = Justified True Belief ❌ ... Phenomenal Evidence ❌ ... Transparency of Rationality ❌ ... Luminosity of Mental States ❌ ... Recommendation: Integrate ... into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2
a_rows_sample.statement: Final recommendation table adopts all seven listed concepts (Knowledge First, Evidence=Knowledge, Factive Mental States, Non-Luminosity, Margin for Error, Anti-KK, Knowledge Rule for Assertion) unconditionally (all checked, no [PROP]/[OPEN] hedging) and recommends integrating them directly into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2 -- a materially stronger, less-hedged recommendation than the same-day review (S2528), which instead treats most of these as PROP-status research candidates and explicitly places 'Evidence=Knowledge' on its own rejection list.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Cases in which p is known can be separated from cases in which p is false by a buffer of true-but-unknown cases. ... Known(p)\Rightarrow Margin(p,\Gamma)>0 ... the required margin can vary from point to point and need not be uniform ... Margin \neq Confidence ... Epistemic quality \neq scalar score
b_rows_sample.statement: Margin-for-error candidate: Known(p) => Margin(p,Gamma)>0 (not adopted as a universal law yet), motivating a margin/buffer relation between False, True-Unknown and Known rather than another flat categorical value; explicitly rejects deriving a scalar confidence or KnowledgeLevel in [0,1] from this, since the margin is proposition/environment-dependent and non-uniform.

b_rows_sample.anchor: EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING ... EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED] ... EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP — strong research candidate] ... EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP]
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes an 8-section theory addition 'EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING': EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED], EL.2 Epistemic Non-Transparency [DERIVED], EL.3 Knowledge Iteration [DERIVED], EL.4 Evidence Relativity [PROP], EL.5 Margin of Error [PROP], EL.6 Accessibility (distinguishing Truth/Knowability/Accessibility/ActualKnowledge) [DERIVED], EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP-strong], EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP], consolidating this file's individual candidates into one proposed section.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Do not adopt KnowledgeOS = Williamson's epistemology ... Do not adopt Knowledge = Evidence ... He explicitly says the equation does not amount to an analysis of either concept. ... Do not adopt Sat = Knowledge ... Confidence = Margin ... Unknown = Unknowable ... Contr = Epistemic inconsistency ... Zero = Structural unknowability
b_rows_sample.statement: Explicit rejection list of seven tempting imports: KnowledgeOS=Williamson's-epistemology, Knowledge=Evidence (noting Williamson himself says his E=K thesis is not an analysis of either concept), Sat=Knowledge, Confidence=Margin, Unknown=Unknowable, Contr=EpistemicInconsistency, Zero=StructuralUnknowability -- these remain separate concepts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: What to Adopt: Knowledge First ✅ ... Evidence = Knowledge ✅ ... Factive Mental States ✅ ... Non-Luminosity ✅ ... Margin for Error ✅ ... Anti-KK ✅ ... Knowledge Rule for Assertion ✅ ... What to Reject: Knowledge = Justified True Belief ❌ ... Phenomenal Evidence ❌ ... Transparency of Rationality ❌ ... Luminosity of Mental States ❌ ... Recommendation: Integrate ... into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2
b_rows_sample.statement: Final recommendation table adopts all seven listed concepts (Knowledge First, Evidence=Knowledge, Factive Mental States, Non-Luminosity, Margin for Error, Anti-KK, Knowledge Rule for Assertion) unconditionally (all checked, no [PROP]/[OPEN] hedging) and recommends integrating them directly into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2 -- a materially stronger, less-hedged recommendation than the same-day review (S2528), which instead treats most of these as PROP-status research candidates and explicitly places 'Evidence=Knowledge' on its own rejection list.
