a_rows_sample.anchor: There is no component of K holding the set of recognised dimensions. ... D_t is the smallest missing component. With it, 'not assessed' is D in D_t AND not exists a in A: a.P.D=D -- decidable in O(n). Without it, the statement has no truth-maker.
a_rows_sample.statement: An executed probe (MISSINGNESS-NOT-ASSESSED in THEORY-CONSTRUCTION-TEST.md) shows a never-assessed dimension and an assessed-with-no-result dimension both render identically in K=(A,R) as 'no assertion mentioning that dimension', proving them provably indistinguishable; introducing D_t (the set of currently recognised dimensions) as a component of K makes 'not assessed' decidable in O(n) and is identified as the smallest missing component to close the missingness gap.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A construction score is not a proof of adequacy. A scoring exercise establishes RELATIVE rank among the candidates enumerated; it establishes nothing about whether any candidate is sufficient, and it cannot detect a capability that NO candidate was scored on.
a_rows_sample.statement: The claim that K=Set(Assertion) x R is correct because it scored highest (15/19) against six candidates is challenged on methodological grounds: a comparative score establishes only relative rank among enumerated candidates, never absolute sufficiency, and cannot detect capabilities no candidate was scored on -- exactly the three (uncertainty, non-identifiability, missingness) later shown to be missed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K is a representation whose referent is undeclared. That is why adequacy could only be argued by SCORING AGAINST CAPABILITIES, never by FIDELITY TO A REFERENT.
a_rows_sample.statement: Testing five possible classifications of what K 'is' (ontology, mathematical state, representation, abstraction, domain-specific projection), only 'representation' is defensible, but its referent (the W it represents) is never named in the theory, so adequacy can currently only be judged by capability-scoring rather than fidelity to a declared referent; once Omega:W->O exists, adequacy becomes answerable, but not before.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Three of eleven have no body: dedup (does not exist), Sigma's strength rule, delta's commit case.
a_rows_sample.statement: A table of eleven operations over K (member, add, merge, supersede, contradicts, dedup, Sigma, Gamma, delta, History, Lineage) with signatures, preconditions, postconditions, determinism and failure modes shows three have no defined body: dedup does not exist as an operation, Sigma's strength rule is absent, and delta's body is undefined for the commit case.

a_rows_sample.anchor: id before withdrawal : 86a0330e2b65 / id after withdrawal : a9d84e7a43d8 / SAME? False / R edge (...) now dangles: True ... The theory's identity rule and its mutability rule cannot both hold.
a_rows_sample.statement: Executing kaudit.py shows that because id is declared derived as H(P,e,c,t,Pi) while e.state is declared mutable, withdrawing one evidence item re-keys the assertion's id and breaks every R edge pointing at the old id, violating StructuralValid's own no-dangling clause -- an internal contradiction between the identity rule and the mutability rule in the same field table, worsened by the audit's own addition of a mutable state field to e.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Because Pi is inside id, the same fact from two sources is two assertions. ... K grows without bound under re-observation ... R is not maintained by merge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Executing kaudit.py shows two assertions of the identical proposition from two different sources get distinct ids (because Pi/provenance is inside id), so merge-as-union cannot deduplicate: corroboration becomes indistinguishable from duplication, K grows unboundedly under repeated observation of the same fact, merge's idempotence holds only for byte-identical assertions, and cross-state relations between semantic twins are never created by merge, silently dropping information.

Superseded: a relation in R or in History -- not a value of Sigma. Valid(K): the blocking sub-predicate was state consistency, which needed a vocab
b_rows_sample.statement: Derives the operational consequences of the 3-state Sigma resolution: the Assertion tuple becomes A=(id,P,Sigma,E,tau,Pi) with Sigma restricted to {Unknown,Supported,Refuted}; Gamma (governance) attaches separately to a governance context, not to A; Superseded becomes a relation in R or History rather than a Sigma value; the previously blocked state-consistency sub-predicate of Valid(K) (from S1603/S1605) becomes computable now that Sigma is fixed; Merge/Supersede become well-typed since supersession operates on the relation rather than mutating a status field.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_t shape: relations must live somewhere -- this constrains the container. UL: 24 terms reduce to 3 states + 4 relations + 7 governance + 4 lifecycle. The 'eleven vocabularies' dissolve.
b_rows_sample.statement: Notes a downstream constraint on the still-open K_t shape blocker (B2): since relations (Superseded, Contested, Corroborated, Disputed) now need an explicit home in the container, this constrains what K_t's tuple/shape can be; and restates the overall UL resolution -- the notorious 'eleven competing vocabularies' dissolve into a clean 3+4+7+4 partition (states + relations + governance + lifecycle).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Not Sigma. Sigma is determined at three states by the mathematics and the corpus. The one residue: Gamma's value set ... That is a governance-process question, not a mathematical one, and it does not block the formal theory ... Therefore I am NOT asking the author to decide anything yet.
b_rows_sample.statement: Closes the B1 blocker without escalating to the human author: Sigma itself is now fully derived (not normative), and the only residual open item -- Gamma's own value vocabulary (which governance statuses the domain recognizes) -- is explicitly deferred as a later, non-blocking governance-process question rather than treated as an immediate normative decision, correcting the S1605 escalation of B1 to AUTHOR INPUT REQUIRED.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Downstream effect: B1 is resolved. The next load-bearing gap moves to K_t's shape -- and Section 9 has just constrained it, because relations (R) now provably need a home.
b_rows_sample.statement: Records the downstream effect of closing B1: the single remaining load-bearing (normative) blocker from S1605's matrix becomes B2, K_t's tuple shape -- now further constrained by the requirement that relations R have an explicit home in the container.

The KNOWLEDGEOS-THEORY-DISCOVERY-REPORT Section 2 is
b_rows_sample.statement: Notes G5 (a per-proposition survivor-theory model with source lineage, assumptions, proof status, computability, test evidence, DDD meaning per proposition) was correctly gated behind completing the step sweep in earlier mandates, but that gate has now opened (sweep complete through Step 246) and the artifact was still never produced; the closest approximation is S1605's Section 2, which is not the required per-proposition granularity.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The 198 non-step files -- 42% of the corpus. Includes the Q-series (Q1-Q24) which -- as this session discovered -- contains the assertion layer the whole late corpus lacks. Traced only in STEP-TRACE-B1/B2/B3. No mandate's coverage requirement reaches them, and I flagged this twice without acting on
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies the 198 non-step files (42% of the corpus, including the Q-series Q1-Q24) as the programme's most consequential coverage gap: it was traced only in three STEP-TRACE files, no mandate's coverage requirement reaches it, and it is exactly where this same session's S1605 finding (the assertion layer already established in Q7) was located -- the verifier explicitly notes flagging this coverage hole twice previously without acting on it.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels share the notation 'K_t=(A_t,R_t,E_t,H_t,Z_t,L_t)'

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would not define knowledge as "information that is true." That is far too weak. The better result is that knowledge is a property of a cognitive system's relationship to reality, and therefore it can be measured along several dimensions.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects an implicit prior working definition of knowledge as 'information that is true' as too weak, and redefines knowledge as a property of a cognitive system's relationship to reality, measurable along several dimensions rather than as a single true/false attribute of information.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We can quantify evidence, truth, reliability, uncertainty, coverage, and competence directly. "Knowledge" itself is better treated as a structured construct derived from those measurable properties.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes directly quantifiable epistemic properties (evidence, truth, reliability, uncertainty, coverage, competence) from 'knowledge' itself, which is instead a structured construct derived from those measurable properties rather than a directly measurable primitive.

a_rows_sample.anchor: knowledge was analyzed as justified true belief, but Gettier cases showed that true + justified belief can still be true merely by luck. ... Reliabilist approaches emphasize that the cognitive process producing the belief must be reliably truth-conducive.
a_rows_sample.statement: Summarizes the classical justified-true-belief (JTB) analysis of knowledge, the Gettier problem (true+justified belief can be true merely by luck), and reliabilism's answer (the belief-forming process must be reliably truth-conducive), as external epistemological grounding for the framework that follows.

a_rows_sample.anchor: knowledge is not merely a collection of propositions; epistemic cognition involves procedural norms governing what a cognitive agent should do under particular circumstances.
a_rows_sample.statement: Cites Pollock & Cruz's view that knowledge is not merely a collection of propositions but involves procedural norms governing what a cognitive agent should do under particular circumstances, feeding into the later competence dimension and the language!=knowledge distinction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge != Information != Belief != Truth. Instead: K = truth-connected, justified, reliable cognitive competence ... There is no universally accepted single definition of knowledge. This is a research definition suitable for the program we are building, not a claim that philosophy has settled the issue.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes the boxed working formalization Knowledge != Information != Belief != Truth, and K = truth-connected, justified, reliable cognitive competence, explicitly qualified as a research working definition for this program, not a claim that philosophy has settled what knowledge is.
a_rows_sample.type_signature: K = truth-connected, justified, reliable cognitive competence

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge is not data ... They contain no knowledge merely by existing. ... Knowledge is not information ... information becomes knowledge only when a cognitive system has an appropriate relationship to the proposition ... Knowledge is not belief ... I can believe ... and be wrong. Therefore Belief =/=> Knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes three ground-floor distinctions with examples: knowledge is not data (bare data like '42', 'Berlin', a date contain no knowledge merely by existing); knowledge is not information (information becomes knowledge only via proposition + evidence + truth + appropriate cognitive connection); and knowledge is not belief (a belief such as 'the server is down' can be wrong, so Belief does not imply Knowledge).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose I randomly guess: "The coin will land heads." It lands heads. My proposition is true. But I didn't thereby acquire knowledge. So: Truth =/=> Knowledge. This is the epistemic luck problem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Knowledge is not Truth alone, via the coin-flip example: a randomly guessed true proposition does not constitute knowledge, illustrating the epistemic-luck problem (Truth does not imply Knowledge).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Truth + Justification =/=> Knowledge without some additional anti-luck condition. ... A system cannot say: "I have evidence, therefore I know." It needs to ask: How did this evidence produce the conclusion, and how robust is that relationship?
a_rows_sample.statement: States the Gettier-derived principle that Truth+Justification does not imply Knowledge without an additional anti-luck condition, and warns systems against the fallacy 'I have evidence, therefore I know' -- they must instead ask how the evidence produced the conclusion and how robust that relationship is; flagged as 'enormously important for KnowledgeOS'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Confidence = 99% does not mean Knowledge = 99%. ... A model can be: highly confident and wrong, uncertain and correct, well calibrated but ignorant, knowledgeable but unable to assign a meaningful scalar confidence. So: Confidence != Knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Knowledge != Confidence, particularly important for AI systems, via four distinguishable failure/success modes: highly confident and wrong, uncertain and correct, well-calibrated but ignorant, and knowledgeable but unable to assign a meaningful scalar confidence.

a_rows_sample.anchor: It distinguishes Smriti, knowledge that is remembered and can change, from Shruti, presented within that tradition as revealed knowledge regarded as unchanging. For our scientific/engineering model, we should not adopt the metaphysical claim that Shruti is objectively infallible. ... remembering a proposition != knowing why / whether it is true. A database can memorize 10 million facts. That does not mean it has knowledge of 10 million facts.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Knowledge != Memorization, drawing on the uploaded Sri Vidya text's Smriti (remembered, changeable knowledge) vs Shruti (claimed unchanging revealed knowledge) distinction, while explicitly declining to adopt the metaphysical claim that Shruti is objectively infallible; illustrates with a database that can memorize 10 million facts without thereby having knowledge of them.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A person can know how to ride a bicycle without being able to formulate the relevant knowledge linguistically. Pollock & Cruz distinguish competence from performance and treat procedural knowledge as something that governs action, not merely verbal description. Therefore: Language != Knowledge. Language is one representation channel for knowledge. That is highly relevant to our Zero/Dhatu research.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Knowledge != Language via the bicycle-riding example and Pollock & Cruz's competence/performance distinction (procedural knowledge governs action, not merely verbal description); language is characterized as one representation channel for knowledge, explicitly flagged as relevant to the batch's Zero/Dhatu research.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A completely internally consistent system can still be wrong. ... A -> B -> C -> D -> A. Perfect coherence. Zero contact with reality. Coherentist epistemology itself recognizes that coherence and truth must not simply be conflated. Thus: Coherence != Truth and therefore: Coherence != Knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Knowledge != Coherence alone, via a counterexample of a perfectly circularly-coherent belief system (A->B->C->D->A) with zero contact with reality, noting that coherentist epistemology itself warns against conflating coherence with truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: "My professor said it." is not itself knowledge. Authority may be evidence. But: Authority != Truth and: Authority != Justification unless the authority relationship itself is appropriately reliable. This becomes especially important for KnowledgeOS because provenance must not be confused with epistemic validity.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Knowledge != Authority: an authority-based claim is not itself knowledge; authority may serve as evidence, but Authority != Truth and Authority != Justification unless the authority relationship is itself appropriately reliable; explicitly warns that provenance must not be confused with epistemic validity, calling this especially important for KnowledgeOS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A system might predict: rain tomorrow = yes and be right. But if it has no understanding of why, it might still have predictive competence without propositional knowledge ... Conversely, knowledge can exist without immediate predictive utility. So: Prediction != Knowledge although predictive performance is one powerful way of testing knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Knowledge != mere successful prediction: a correct rain-tomorrow prediction without understanding of why is predictive competence rather than propositional knowledge, and conversely knowledge can exist without immediate predictive utility; predictive performance remains one powerful way of testing knowledge, but is not itself knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: "I know that pressure increases when volume decreases." versus "I understand why pressure increases when volume decreases." Understanding involves relations, structure, explanation and integration. So: Knowledge != Understanding but: Understanding superset-of structured relationships among known elements.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Knowledge != Understanding, contrasting 'I know that P' with 'I understand why P' (pressure/volume example); understanding involves relations, structure, explanation and integration, and is characterized as encompassing structured relationships among known elements, citing the Stanford Encyclopedia's treatment of understanding as a distinct epistemic good.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The book describes the Vijnanamaya Kosha as the layer where sensory perceptions are processed and meaning is imbued through awareness, insight and consciousness; it associates this layer with wisdom and conscious choice. Again, I would treat this as a traditional conceptual model, not as established neuroscience. ... DATA -> INFORMATION -> KNOWLEDGE -> UNDERSTANDING -> WISDOM. And these should not be collapsed.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a five-layer hierarchy DATA -> INFORMATION -> KNOWLEDGE -> UNDERSTANDING -> WISDOM that must not be collapsed, informed by the Sri Vidya source's Vijnanamaya Kosha (a layer associating processed sensory perception with wisdom and conscious choice), explicitly treated as a traditional conceptual model rather than established neuroscience.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge is a sufficiently reliable and non-accidental cognitive capacity to represent some aspect of reality as it is, supported by appropriate evidence or competence, such that the representation remains defensible under relevant challenge and can appropriately guide inference or action. Formally: K(s,p,t) means: subject/system (s) knows proposition (p) at time (t).
a_rows_sample.statement: Formulates a research working definition of knowledge: a sufficiently reliable and non-accidental cognitive capacity to represent some aspect of reality, supported by appropriate evidence/competence, defensible under relevant challenge, and able to appropriately guide inference or action; formalized as K(s,p,t) meaning subject/system s knows proposition p at time t, noted to require several further conditions.
a_rows_sample.type_signature: K(s,p,t) : subject s knows proposition p at time t

a_rows_sample.anchor: Instead of pretending knowledge is one number, define: K = (T,J,R,A,S,C,U) where T=Truth, J=Justification/evidential support, R=Reliability, A=Anti-luck/causal appropriateness, S=Stability under defeaters, C=Competence/ability to use the knowledge, U=Uncertainty. Then knowledge becomes a vector, not a scalar. This is much more defensible.
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces the central Knowledge Vector formalization K=(T,J,R,A,S,C,U) across seven dimensions (Truth, Justification, Reliability, Anti-luck, Stability-under-defeaters, Competence, Uncertainty), establishing the principle that knowledge should be represented as a vector rather than a single scalar number, as more defensible than a one-number knowledge score.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Dimension 1 - Truth ... T = 1 if p true, 0 if p false. For uncertain domains, we can use probability or graded truth models. Dimension 2 - Evidence ... J(p) in [0,1] ... we should not simply average evidence sources. Evidence needs structure ... is stronger than: 100 copies of the same article ... because the latter may represent only one independent evidential source.
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the Truth dimension T (binary or probabilistic/graded for uncertain domains) and the Evidence dimension J(p) in [0,1] incorporating independent observations/provenance/source quality/experimental replication/logical derivation/measurement quality/temporal relevance; warns that evidence sources must not simply be averaged because evidence needs structure, illustrated by contrasting a structured two-observation inference chain against 100 copies of the same article, which may represent only one independent evidential source.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Let a cognitive process (f) have: R(f)=P(true output | f). For example: thermometer: R = 0.998, random guess: R ~= 0.50. Reliabilism explicitly treats truth-conduciveness of the belief-forming process as epistemically important.
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the Reliability dimension R(f)=P(true output | f) for a cognitive/measurement process f, grounded directly in reliabilist epistemology, illustrated by a thermometer (R=0.998) versus a random guess (R~=0.50).

b_rows_sample.anchor: How does a knowledge system distinguish source, means, validation, and realization? ... Knowledge is not one entity -- it has an epistemic pipeline.
b_rows_sample.statement: The Veda-Upanishad-Vedanta analysis is framed as distinct from prior lenses (Topology/Vani/Zero/Gita-Tripuisi/ECS) because it asks how a knowledge system distinguishes source, means, validation, and realization -- introducing the claim that knowledge is not one entity but has an epistemic pipeline.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Source -> Essence extraction -> Interpretation / validation method ... A common mistake in AI systems: Document = Knowledge. Vedanta would reject that.
b_rows_sample.statement: The Veda->Upanishad->Vedanta structure is abstracted as Source->Essence extraction->Interpretation/validation method; warns against the common AI-system mistake of equating Document with Knowledge (better model: Expression->Meaning extraction->Understanding->Validated knowledge).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Pramata (Knower) / Pramana (Validation method) / Prameya (Object known) / Prama (Valid knowledge). This is almost a missing KnowledgeOS primitive.
b_rows_sample.statement: Pramana (means of knowledge) is proposed as the biggest useful concept from Vedanta: it separates Pramata (Knower), Pramana (Validation method), Prameya (Object known), Prama (Valid knowledge). Proposes a 'Knowledge Claim' primitive with fields Object (what is claimed), Source (origin), Method (how established), Validator (who/what validated), State (current epistemic status), replacing a naive Knowledge{content, metadata} structure.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS may need: Operational Knowledge / Meta-Knowledge ... A system that only stores operational knowledge becomes a documentation system. KnowledgeOS needs knowledge about knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Structural (not literal) borrowing of the Apara Vidya (lower knowledge: facts/sciences/methods/texts) vs Para Vidya (higher knowledge: knowledge of underlying principle) distinction, yielding Operational Knowledge vs Meta-Knowledge; warns that a system storing only operational knowledge degenerates into a documentation system.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Reality -> Observation -> Evidence -> Validation method -> Knowledge claim -> Authority decision -> Published knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Combines ECS ('epistemic systems govern belief, not reality') with Vedanta ('knowledge requires a valid means of knowing') into a stronger seven-stage pipeline: Reality->Observation->Evidence->Validation method->Knowledge claim->Authority decision->Published knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Vedanta adds: Meaning != Valid Knowledge. Because a statement can have meaning but still not be valid. Example: "The server is healthy"
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends the Vani lens (Expression != Meaning) with a Vedanta addition (Meaning != Valid Knowledge). Worked example: "The server is healthy" separates Expression (text exists), Meaning (a health condition is described), Validation (monitoring evidence confirms it), Authority (authorized person/system accepts it) as four distinct, separable layers.

b_rows_sample.anchor: INV-KOS Candidate: Knowledge Requires Provenance of Knowing. A KnowledgeOS knowledge state SHALL preserve not only what is known, but the means by which it became knowable. Forbidden collapse: Statement -> Truth / Source document -> Valid knowledge. Strength: Candidate.
b_rows_sample.statement: New candidate invariant proposed (not yet established): 'Knowledge Requires Provenance of Knowing' -- a KnowledgeOS knowledge state should preserve not only what is known but the means (Claim/Evidence/Method/Validator/Authority) by which it became knowable; forbids collapsing a Statement into Truth or a Source document into Valid knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: How does a knowledge system distinguish source, means, validation, and realization? ... Knowledge is not one entity -- it has an epistemic pipeline.
b_rows_sample.statement: Finalized/placed version of S0213's framing: the Vedanta lens distinguishes source, means, validation, realization, adding an epistemic-pipeline view of knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Pramata (Knower) / Pramana (Validation method) / Prameya (Object known) / Prama (Valid knowledge). Almost a missing KnowledgeOS primitive.
b_rows_sample.statement: Pramana/Knowledge Claim primitive restated in the placed document (Object/Source/Method/Validator/State fields).

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS may need: Operational Knowledge / Meta-Knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Apara Vidya/Para Vidya-derived Operational Knowledge vs Meta-Knowledge distinction restated in the placed document.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Vedanta adds: Meaning != Valid Knowledge. Example: "The server is healthy"
b_rows_sample.statement: Meaning != Valid Knowledge extension restated with the 'server is healthy' worked example (Expression/Meaning/Validation/Authority as separable layers).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Reality -> Observation -> Pramana (valid method) -> Knowledge state -> Authority/publication
b_rows_sample.statement: Combined ECS+Vedanta pipeline restated in the placed document.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Vedanta | Knowing requires a valid means
b_rows_sample.statement: Final lens-contributions synthesis table (EKS/PKS/AIP/Topology/Vani/Zero/Gita/Vedanta/ECS) restated, with Vedanta's row bolded as 'Knowing requires a valid means'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A knowledge space can contain fundamentally different modes of knowing, not merely more or fewer dimensions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reads Para Vidya vs Apara Vidya (higher/lower knowledge) not as a ranking to import into KnowledgeOS, but as evidence that a knowledge space can hold fundamentally different MODES of knowing (e.g. knowing phenomena vs knowing substrate/principle) — a change in kind, not merely 'Knowledge = dimensions × values'.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'knowledge-vector-measurement-framework' POSSIBLY relates to 'vedanta-pramana-epistemic-pipeline' (batch B0012). Note: Combines classical epistemology (JTB, Gettier, reliabilism, Pollock & Cruz's procedural/defeater theory) with a Sri Vidya source text (Smriti/Shruti, Vijnanamaya Kosha, 'knowledge is one but understood in ten ways') to reject 'knowledge = true information' and propose knowledge as a multi-dimensional, quantifiable, non-scalar construct: a Knowledge Vector K=(Truth,Justification,Reliability,Anti-luck,Stability-under-defeaters,Competence,Uncertainty); formalizes reliability R(f)=P(true output|f), counterfactual robustness CR(p), defeater resistance DR(p) (rebutting vs undercutting defeaters), competence via held-out task performance, and an information-gain uncertainty measure with an explicit warning that entropy/mutual information are not automatically epistemic-knowledge measures; proposes a composite scalar K* explicitly as a decision-oriented projection of the canonical vector, never a replacement for it; introduces a 'KNOWLEDGE CLAIM' epistemic-object ontology (proposition+evidence+provenance+justification+inference-path+reliability+defeaters+counterfactual-tests+temporal-validity+competence-evidence+uncertainty) replacing a flat document/fact/embedding ontology; derives Knowledge Invariance KI (agreement across independent representations), and amount-of-knowledge quantities (Coverage KC, Reliability KR, Depth, Robustness KB, Transfer KT) rendered as a 'Knowledge Profile' report card rather than one scalar; states knowledge decay (K(p,t1)!=K(p,t2)) and time-indexing; validates (per the source's own claim) the existing observation-vs-knowledge-claim architectural distinction; ties into the batch's Dhatu hypothesis by reframing knowledge acquisition as a transformation pipeline rather than a static object; closes by recommending a formal 15-part 'Knowledge Ontology & Measurement Framework v1.0' deliverable mapping to Zero/Dhatu and to KnowledgeOS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate kernel concepts include: Identity, Context, Provenance, Time, Contract, Requirement, KnowledgeState, History, Relation, EpistemicStatus. ... A common architectural failure is to place every domain concept into a shared kernel.
a_rows_sample.statement: 18.8: proposes a small candidate semantic kernel shared across bounded contexts (Identity, Context, Provenance, Time, Contract, Requirement, KnowledgeState, History, Relation, EpistemicStatus) and warns that placing every domain concept into a shared kernel creates a 'distributed conceptual monolith'; a concept belongs in the kernel only when its semantics are genuinely shared and stable enough to justify shared ownership.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The kernel creates the ecosystem; the company creates value around the ecosystem.
b_rows_sample.statement: Uses the Linux/Red Hat precedent to argue KnowledgeOS's moat is the kernel plus governance plus evidence model (not the AI model, which is commoditized), proposing a Community/Professional/Enterprise revenue-tier structure and a 10-year IPO roadmap.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS Kernel = the minimal system responsible for creating, identifying, relating, governing, and preserving organizational knowledge objects.
b_rows_sample.statement: The proposed load-bearing definition of the 'KnowledgeOS Kernel', explicitly modeled after the Linux kernel's separation from applications: the kernel provides knowledge primitives (Identity, Lifecycle, Evidence, Authority) and must not know about specific technologies (SAP, Kubernetes, Jira).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Linus did not start by designing 'the operating system of the world.' He started by solving a concrete problem, created a small working kernel ... 'Can we create a trusted kernel that allows digitalization robots to operate safely?'
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS should not start with an AI-driven Digitalization Robot ambition; the correct starting question is the smallest trusted kernel that later allows robots to operate safely, mirroring Linux's incremental 0.01-kernel-first history.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Open-source the KnowledgeOS Kernel. Commercialize the Digitalization Robot Platform.
b_rows_sample.statement: Recommends an open-core business model (open KnowledgeOS Kernel for trust/ecosystem, commercial Digitalization Robot/Enterprise Platform for revenue), by analogy with Linux Kernel vs Red Hat Enterprise Linux.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Linux manages computer resources. KnowledgeOS manages organizational intelligence resources ... which knowledge is valid, who owns it, and how can it be trusted?
b_rows_sample.statement: States the deepest claimed difference between the Linux and KnowledgeOS kernel analogies: Linux answers 'which process can access which resource', while KnowledgeOS must answer 'which knowledge is valid, who owns it, and how can it be trusted.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Rust for the KnowledgeOS Kernel, Kotlin/Spring for the Enterprise Runtime, Python for Intelligence, TypeScript for Experience.
b_rows_sample.statement: Recommends a multi-language technology stack (Rust kernel for memory-safety/correctness, Kotlin+Spring Boot enterprise runtime, Python intelligence layer, TypeScript studio/frontend) with an estimated 12-18 month timeline for a first Kernel v1.0 with a small expert team.

b_rows_sample.anchor: If you want IPO potential, do not position KnowledgeOS as 'AI chatbot' ... nor 'Documentation tool' ... Position as: The operating system for enterprise knowledge and digital transformation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues the commercial positioning category determines addressable market size; 'AI chatbot' is too easy to copy, 'documentation tool' is too small a category for IPO ambitions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Kernel scope: 'minimal kernel, no AI' (S0167) vs the platform vision where an AI-driven Digitalization Robot is the top layer (S0171) — the corpus itself frames the robot as a distribution, keeping the kernel AI-free, so the tension is scope of the 'core' vs the 'product'.
b_rows_sample.statement: Surfaces T1: a minimal AI-free kernel proposal versus an AI-driven robot as the platform's top execution layer, resolved by the corpus's own framing (robot = distribution, kernel stays AI-free) but not formally decided.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Rust · Spring Boot · Gradle/Cargo · microservices · plugin architecture · Event Sourcing · Kafka are recommendations/hypotheses in the corpus, never adopted KnowledgeOS technology.
b_rows_sample.statement: Explicit preservation note keeping every named technology recommendation level-tagged as a hypothesis, never promoted to adopted architecture, while noting the existing PHP/Laravel + TypeScript/Vue platform is the ESTABLISHED current stack.

b_rows_sample.anchor: DI principle vs framework import: adopt the DI/composition-root principle without adopting Spring — the corpus wants the first, but the kernel file pairs the principle with the Spring runtime.
b_rows_sample.statement: Surfaces T4: the DI-principle proposal explicitly wants the principle without the Spring framework, yet the kernel-technology brainstorm pairs the same principle with a recommended Spring/Kotlin runtime.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KNOWLEDGEOS KERNEL protects: identity · evidence · provenance · lifecycle · authority · invariants · temporal state / higher layers provide: assurance · analytics · inference · simulation · AI · visualization · delivery ... a PROPOSED KERNEL BOUNDARY CANDIDATE, outline supported, provenance+temporal weak.
b_rows_sample.statement: H-10: tests the seven-concern kernel/higher-layer split against all three baselines per-concern; identity, evidence, lifecycle, authority, and invariants are supported, provenance and temporal state are weak, so the overall split is a candidate outline, not an established fact.

b_rows_sample.anchor: WHAT IS THE CORE DOMAIN ACT? ... Verification | Admission | Determination | Transformation | Epistemic Maintenance | Justification Preservation | Constitutional Transition
b_rows_sample.statement: Seven alternative formulations of KnowledgeOS's core domain act are compared (Verification, Admission, Determination, Transformation, Epistemic Maintenance, Justification Preservation, Constitutional Transition), each with its domain-meaning implication.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The core domain act is the constitutionally-gated transition from candidate to admissible knowledge state.
b_rows_sample.statement: Hypothesis: the Kernel's core domain act is the constitutionally-gated transition from candidate to admissible knowledge state, combining a candidate, a gate (constitutional rules), a verdict (admissibility), and a state change.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A knowledge claim cannot exist without: identity, evidence, justification, epistemic state, confidence, and history.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposed aggregate invariant: a knowledge claim cannot exist without identity, evidence, justification, epistemic state, confidence, and history all present and consistent together; the Kernel is framed as 'the guardian of this aggregate invariant.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate -> Verification -> Admissibility -> Identity -> Epistemic State -> Knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Admission is modelled as a distinction chain (Candidate -> Verification[well-formed?] -> Admissibility[constitution?] -> Identity[stable anchor?] -> Epistemic State -> Knowledge) and as an 8-step process from candidate proposal to emission of KnowledgeCreated.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Identity assignment | ESSENTIAL ... Semantic interpretation | NOT ESSENTIAL ... Reasoning | NOT ESSENTIAL ... Workflow | NOT ESSENTIAL ... Projection | NOT ESSENTIAL
b_rows_sample.statement: A capability table classifies identity assignment, evidence admission, justification preservation, epistemic-state determination, confidence assignment, history recording, and constitutional evaluation as ESSENTIAL (each tied to a named invariant); candidate verification as SUPPORTING; and semantic interpretation, reasoning, workflow, and projection as NOT ESSENTIAL to the Kernel's minimum domain capacity.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Natural-language interpretation | Parsing | Normalization | Canonicalization | Reasoning | Candidate generation | Retrieval | Search | Ranking | Model inference | Orchestration | Workflow | Projection | UI | Infrastructure | Evidence acquisition
b_rows_sample.statement: A 15-item table enumerates responsibilities that belong OUTSIDE the Kernel, each with a DDD reason: natural-language interpretation, parsing, normalization, canonicalization, reasoning, candidate generation, retrieval, search, ranking, model inference, orchestration, workflow, projection, UI, infrastructure, and evidence acquisition -- summarized as the principle that the Kernel is representation-agnostic and does not perform semantic interpretation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The Kernel is a domain boundary, not a component.
b_rows_sample.statement: Six candidate interpretations of what the Kernel 'is' are compared (aggregate boundary, domain decision boundary, admission boundary, consistency boundary, constitutional boundary, small domain core inside the aggregate); concludes the Kernel is best understood as the admission boundary + consistency boundary -- a conceptual domain boundary, not an implementation component, though it may be implemented inside the aggregate.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeCreated is the domain event that signals the completion of admission.
b_rows_sample.statement: KnowledgeCreated is analyzed as the domain event signalling completion of admission -- the business moment the candidate becomes part of KnowledgeOS with identity, evidence, justification, epistemic state, confidence, and history all established; the Kernel's job is to produce this event on success and nothing/a rejection on failure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONSTITUTIONAL KERNEL <- the eleven articles (PRESERVE) ... Engine Layer (GOVERN) ... Mechanisms (GOVERN) ... Representations (ENABLE) ... Implementation (ENABLE)
a_rows_sample.statement: Chapter III, the Kernel Boundary: a 5-tier diagram -- Constitutional Kernel (the 11 articles, PRESERVE) served by Engine Layer (validation engines, fallacy detection, debate pipeline, intent classification, verdict vocabulary, GOVERN), Mechanisms (epistemic-inquiry lifecycle, reasoning pipelines, GOVERN), Representations (evidence records, context tuples, epistemic state model, absence taxonomy, epistemic graph, typed encodings, ENABLE), and Implementation (storage, interfaces, systems, deliberately unconstrained, ENABLE). III.2 no engine/mechanism/representation may violate an article -- evolution that violates an article is a corruption, not an evolution, subject to Chapter V. III.3 implementation is deliberately out of constitutional scope.

a_rows_sample.anchor: V.1 Engineering evolution -- no amendment required. ... V.2 Constitutional amendment -- required ... V.3 What amendment MAY do ... V.4 Ratification.
a_rows_sample.statement: Chapter V, Amendment Discipline (new content, not present verbatim in any prior artifact in this file group): engines/mechanisms/representations/implementation (Chapter III) MAY evolve freely provided no evolution violates an article (V.1); the 11 articles, the character, the negative boundary, and the kernel/engine boundary SHALL NOT change except by HPA-ratified constitutional amendment, and no article SHALL be weakened (V.2); amendment MAY refine wording, correct inconsistency, or -- on evidence a specific corruption is unguarded -- add a strengthening clause, but SHALL NOT add new concepts/sources/rows ('the corpus that produced this Constitution is closed; adding knowledge to the kernel would violate the discipline this Constitution establishes', V.3); amendment is effective only by HPA ruling following the same evidence/domain-independence/necessity/failure-test discipline that produced step 5 (V.4).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge != Decision != Action; decision problem D=(K,A,Θ,U,C,R); expected utility argmax rule not a universal formula
a_rows_sample.statement: States Knowledge != Decision != Action: a decision needs objective, alternatives, constraints, risk, utility, authority beyond mere knowledge. Formalizes a decision problem D=(K,A,Theta,U,C,R) (knowledge, available actions, world states, utility, constraints, risk model), expected utility EU(a|K)=sum_theta P(theta|K)U(a,theta) (or the integral form), and the rule a*=argmax_a EU(a|K) -- explicitly qualified: this is not universally the correct decision rule (alternatives include minimax, constrained optimization, risk-sensitive utility, satisficing, lexicographic priorities, regulatory rules), so DecisionPolicy != UniversalMathematicalFormula; the Decision Context owns the meaning of DecisionPolicy, the mathematics supplies tools, the domain determines which is legitimate -- 'prevents mathematics from silently becoming business policy'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiments 1-5: underdetermined decision returns InsufficientDecisionBasis; ties; hard constraints vs preferences; risk limits; governance prohibition overrides utility
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: given K and A but no utility function, ChooseAction(K,A) must return Underdetermined/InsufficientDecisionBasis rather than inventing a decision -- PASS. Experiment 2: EU(a1)=EU(a2) yields a Tie, requiring an explicit tie-breaking rule if selection is mandatory -- PASS. Experiment 3: EU(a1)>EU(a2) but a1 not-in FeasibleActions means a1 cannot be selected; defines A_feasible={a in A: C(a)=True}, a*=argmax over A_feasible -- PASS, giving BestAction = BestFeasibleAction under the applicable decision policy, not simply HighestUtilityAction, and Constraint != Preference (a hard constraint C(a)=False removes a from A_feasible entirely, a preference only affects utility). Experiment 4: a risk policy Risk(a)<=R_max makes a high-EU action ineligible if it violates the risk limit -- PASS. Experiment 5: governance marking Forbidden(a1)=True excludes a high-utility a1 from A_feasible -- PASS, giving Decision = Knowledge + Objective + Constraints + Policy, and framing KnowledgeOS's question as 'what decisions are legitimate under knowledge, objectives, constraints, and authority' rather than a pure optimizer's max f(x).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision provenance object; risk measures (variance, VaR/ES) as domain-chosen, not universal
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines an auditable decision basis D=(KnowledgeSnapshot, Alternatives, Objective, Constraints, Policy, Model, SelectedAction, Rationale), with Rationale = f(Knowledge, Evidence, Policy, Objective, Risk), not merely 'AI recommended action A'. Notes a high-EU-but-catastrophic-downside action may be disfavored versus a slightly-lower-EU low-variance alternative by a risk-sensitive policy such as EU(a)-lambda*Var(U(a)), or domain-specific measures VaR_alpha/ES_alpha for financial-like domains -- 'KnowledgeOS should not impose one universal risk measure'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: AI proposal is not decision; proposal strength != decision authority (experiments 6-7)
a_rows_sample.statement: AIProposal -> DecisionEvaluation is retained (a proposal is not yet a Decision). Experiment 6: AI proposes a forbidden action a_f; Decision=Rejected -- PASS. Experiment 7: AI proposes a1 without sufficient decision basis; DecisionStatus=InsufficientBasis, not Approved -- PASS. Gives the epistemic boundary: Proposal strength != Decision authority.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Probability thresholds as policy, not mathematical truth; threshold sensitivity and robust (minimax) decision-making under model-set uncertainty
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: threshold=0.95, P(p)=0.94 gives ActionNotAuthorized -- PASS; notes a threshold is a policy, not a mathematical truth. Notes threshold-crossing at P(p)=0.951 may still be domain-prohibited if the uncertainty estimate is large, so a probability threshold alone may be insufficient. Introduces robust decision-making over a model set M (rather than optimizing a single expected value): a*=argmax_a min_{M in M} EU_M(a), 'a possible decision policy, not a universal one'. Distinguishes Aleatoric uncertainty (irreducible variability, e.g. manufacturing process randomness) from Epistemic uncertainty (incomplete knowledge/model limitations, e.g. little data about a new machine) -- additional measurements may reduce the latter but not the former.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EVSI makes information acquisition itself a governed decision; a controlled decision-learning loop; not all knowledge is decision-relevant
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Expected Value of Sample Information EVSI = EU_with-sample - EU_current, and asks whether EVSI > cost(E) before acquiring additional measurement E, making information acquisition itself a decision. Formalizes the resulting loop K_t -> D_info -> E_new -> K_{t+1} as 'not a problematic cycle... a controlled decision-learning loop' giving KnowledgeOS active-learning capability. Experiment 10 (EVSI=0, positive acquisition cost): rational policy may choose not to acquire the information -- PASS, reinforcing Step 61: information can have IG>0 but EVSI=0, so not all knowledge is decision-relevant. Experiment 11: modest IG but large EVSI (an information source changes the optimal action despite modest uncertainty reduction) -- PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Richer typed Decision object; Selected != Authorized; Decision selection != Authorization; complete governed chain
a_rows_sample.statement: Strengthens Decision = (DecisionId, KnowledgeSnapshot, Objective, Alternatives, Constraints, Policy, RiskModel, DecisionRule, SelectedAlternative, Authority), 'much richer than decision=approve'. Decision status can be Proposed, Evaluated, Selected, Rejected, Expired, Superseded -- but Selected != Authorized: the system can determine a*=best feasible alternative without granting execution permission, giving Decision selection != Authorization. Experiment 12: Selected(a1)=True but Authorized(a1)=False must block execution -- PASS. Notes even Authorized(a1) does not mean Executed(a1) (a separate transition), giving the complete chain Knowledge -> Evaluation -> Decision -> Authorization -> Action -> Outcome, each arrow governed. States AI participates at multiple points (EvidenceExtraction, Hypothesis, DecisionProposal, RiskAnalysis) but none automatically implies AuthorizedAction: AI = Agent capable of producing governed artifacts, not AI = Authority.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Adversarial/objective-manipulation attacks rejected; objective versioning as a governance requirement
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 13: an AI intentionally recommends a_bad due to a misaligned objective; the decision policy's utility/constraint evaluation rejects it -- PASS. Notes a harder attack -- silently replacing the objective itself (e.g. MaximizeProfit -> MaximizeAgentReward) -- is not an ordinary decision error but a governance violation, requiring objectives that matter to be versioned and governed: an ObjectiveVersion with a decision's ObjectiveRef(D), enabling historical evaluation of D1 against O1. Experiment 14: D1 created under O1, O2 later activated; historical ObjectiveRef(D1)=O1 is retained -- PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Multi-objective weighted utility as a governance surface, never hidden in a prompt; unauthorized-weight-change rejection
a_rows_sample.statement: For multi-objective utility U = w1*U1 + w2*U2 + w3*U3 (e.g. cost/quality/risk), states the weights w_i are themselves governance choices: 'UtilityModel is part of decision governance when consequential. It should not be hidden inside an AI prompt.' Experiment 15: an AI changes w1 from 0.4 to 0.9 without authorization; the decision should reject the ungoverned utility model -- PASS, illustrating a deeper form of AI governance: governing not only AI output but also the DecisionModel and Objective.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision reproducibility bounded by computational-dependency reproducibility; missing model version rejected
a_rows_sample.statement: States DecisionReplay should reproduce a decision given K_t,O,C,P,M,D_R when deterministic semantics apply; for stochastic (AI/Monte Carlo) models, exact reproducibility may require RandomSeed and ModelVersion, and where exact reproduction is impossible the system should preserve relevant computational metadata (ModelId, ModelVersion, Prompt/ConfigurationRef, InputSnapshot, ComputationStatus). Gives the principle: a consequential decision should be reproducible to the extent its computational dependencies are reproducible. Experiment 16: a decision referencing Model=M with no version becomes ambiguous once the model changes, so it should be rejected or marked non-reproducible per policy -- PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision sensitivity/local robustness analysis; DecisionRobustness more informative than DecisionConfidence
a_rows_sample.statement: Notes DecisionConfidence alone is insufficient; proposes DecisionRobustness/sensitivity analysis. Example: a1 optimal for P(p)>0.55, a2 optimal below; at P(p)=0.56 the decision is highly sensitive (SensitivityHigh). Defines local robustness: D(K)=a is robust if D(K')=a for all K' in a neighborhood N(K). Experiment 17: a small perturbation P(p): 0.56->0.54 flips a1->a2, so the system records high sensitivity -- PASS. Notes this is more useful for human governance than a bare confidence percentage: 'A is selected under the current model, but the decision is highly sensitive to a small change in the relevant assumption.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: OutcomeQuality != DecisionQuality; decision calibration across many decisions
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates BadOutcome ⇏ BadDecision: a rational decision (e.g. P(success)=0.9) can still produce a bad outcome, so OutcomeQuality != DecisionQuality. Over many decisions D1,...,Dn, ExpectedUtility can be compared against RealizedUtility for empirical feedback, and DecisionCalibration becomes possible (e.g. among decisions predicted P(success)=0.8, ~80% should succeed if calibrated) -- 'calibration again'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Four new invariants: I_DecisionAuthority, I_DecisionBasis, I_ActionBoundary, I_ObjectiveIntegrity
a_rows_sample.statement: Adds four named invariants: I_DecisionAuthority (knowledge alone cannot authorize an action); I_DecisionBasis (every consequential decision references the knowledge, policy, objective, and computational basis required by its domain); I_ActionBoundary (decision selection does not imply execution); I_ObjectiveIntegrity (consequential decision objectives cannot be silently modified by an ungoverned agent).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Step 62 verdict: decision-making as its own bounded semantic layer; five-layer synthesis; opens Step 63 on causal reasoning/intervention
a_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 62 -- PASS with the refinement that KnowledgeOS must treat decision-making as its own bounded semantic layer between knowledge and authorization. Synthesizes five layers (Knowledge, Objective, DecisionPolicy, Authorization, Action) and the chain K + Objective + Constraints + Risk + Policy -> Decision -> (+ Authority + CurrentGovernance) -> Authorization -> (+ ExecutionPolicy) -> Action -> Outcome. Updates the running pipeline to Observation -> Evidence -> Knowledge -> Information -> Decision -> Authorization -> Action -> Outcome -> Learning. Opens Step 63 (Causal Reasoning and Intervention): distinguishing P(Y|X) from P(Y|do(X)) as 'absolutely central for KnowledgeOS' since a model may correctly learn P(Y|X) while still making the wrong decision about do(X) -- to investigate causal graphs, interventions, counterfactuals, treatment effects, confounding, mediation, causal evidence, causal assumptions, and the prediction/intervention boundary, framed as testing whether KnowledgeOS is a governed computational knowledge-and-decision system rather than merely an AI knowledge repository.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Structured CausalEstimate object with mandatory fully-specified Estimand; effect heterogeneity; CausalEffect != DecisionUtility
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines CE=(Treatment,Outcome,Estimand,Population,Method,Assumptions,Data,ModelVersion,Estimate,Uncertainty) as a structured causal result object. Requires Estimand to be fully specified (on whom, over what time, under what intervention, measured how, average or subgroup effect) -- 'effect of X on Y is incomplete'. Restates causal effect heterogeneity (ATE=0.2 can hide ATE_groupA=0.8 vs ATE_groupB=-0.1, so AverageEffect≠UniversalEffect, requiring Population scope preservation) and CausalEffect≠DecisionUtility (a positive effect can still yield negative net utility once cost is included), and reiterates temporal precedence alone is insufficient for causal direction (TemporalPrecedence ⇏ Causality).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Probability != Decision (identical success probability, different stakes yield different rational actions); Utility != Evidence; decision function D:(K,C,P,U,R)
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: P(Success|A)=0.8 identical across Case A (+100/-10) and Case B (+10/-1000) yields very different rational decisions -- Probability != Decision. Re-derives expected utility EU(A)=sum P(O_i|do(A))U(O_i); experiment 1 computes EU(A)=76 correctly. States utility is a preference/objective, not an empirical property -- Utility != Evidence; experiment 2 rejects inferring P(A)=High from U(A)=100. Defines the decision function D:(K,C,P,U,R) -> Decision (knowledge, context, policy, utility, risk constraints), 'considerably more accurate than AI->Decision'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Optimization within the feasible policy space; Decision != Authorization re-confirmed (experiments 3-4)
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: EU(A)=90>EU(B)=70 but Policy(A)=Forbidden correctly yields Decision=B -- PASS, confirming optimization occurs inside the feasible policy space (A*=argmax over A_allowed). Experiment 4: KnowledgeOS determining A*=Deploy while the executing agent lacks deployment authority correctly yields Decision=ApprovedPreference but Authorization=Denied -- PASS, reconfirming Decision != Authorization as 'one of our most important architectural boundaries'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Risk = Probability×Consequence approximation; catastrophic-low-probability rejection; hard constraint vs preference re-derived
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives Risk = Probability x Consequence as a basic approximation (real models may add exposure, uncertainty, detectability, reversibility, systemic effects). Experiment 5: P=0.001, Loss=-100M, policy forbidding catastrophic risk correctly yields ActionRejected despite low expected loss -- PASS. Re-derives hard constraint (A not-in A_allowed, eliminates alternatives) versus preference (U(A)>U(B), ranks them); experiment 6: two legally permissible actions with U(A)>U(B) yields A preferred but not mandatory -- PASS. Formalizes decision as constrained optimization: max_a U(a) subject to C_1(a),...,C_n(a)=True.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EvidenceConflict != ValueConflict; stakeholder utility disagreement is not disguised as a factual conflict
a_rows_sample.statement: Notes utility itself may be uncertain/contested: different stakeholders may assign U_A(a)!=U_B(a), so there may be no single objectively correct decision without specifying whose utility applies. Experiment 7: stakeholder A preferring A and stakeholder B preferring B, both legitimate under their declared objectives, correctly yields PreferenceConflict -- PASS, 'should not disguise a value conflict as a factual conflict'. States EvidenceConflict != ValueConflict ('Action A is likely to save 1M' is epistemic; 'saving 1M justifies this risk' is a value/policy question). Experiment 8: strong evidence for A rejected by stakeholders on ethical-cost grounds correctly yields KnowledgeSupports(A) while DecisionRejects(A) -- PASS, 'exactly how the architecture should behave'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Robust worst-case decision-making under interval-valued probability; distributional model uncertainty preserved
a_rows_sample.statement: For P(Success) in [0.6,0.9] (rather than a point estimate), a robust decision may consider the worst case min_{p in [0.6,0.9]} EU(A,p). Experiment 9: a probability interval correctly yields a decision based on a declared robust/risk policy rather than pretending P=0.8 is exact -- PASS. Notes E[X]=10 with unknown full distribution P(X) makes risk calculations sensitive to distributional assumptions, which KnowledgeOS should preserve. Experiment 10: two models (normality vs heavy tails) fitting data reasonably well but giving substantially different risk estimates correctly keeps ModelUncertainty visible -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Vector-valued utility; Pareto dominance and frontier; Optimization != Preference
b_rows_sample.statement: Replaces scalar U(a) with vector U(a)=(U_1(a),...,U_n(a)) (e.g. Cost/Quality/Risk/CustomerValue/Compliance). Defines Pareto dominance: A dominates B if U_i(A)>=U_i(B) for all i and U_j(A)>U_j(B) for at least one j. Experiment 1: A=(100,100) dominating B=(80,90) lets B be eliminated without any stakeholder weighting -- PASS, 'mathematically important because some decisions can be simplified without imposing subjective preferences'. Defines the Pareto frontier P={a in A : no b in A with b succ a}. Experiment 2: A=(100,40), B=(80,80), C=(50,100), none dominating, all remain on the frontier -- PASS. States the system can prove B is not dominated but not that B is 'best' -- selecting among Pareto-optimal alternatives requires a value judgment or policy: Optimization != Preference.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Weighted utility; WeightSelection is itself a governed artifact; DecisionModel as a first-class artifact
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a weighted-utility policy U(a)=sum w_i U_i(a), w_i>=0 (often summing to 1), a*=argmax U(a). States weights are not mathematical facts -- 'WeightSelection is itself a governed artifact'. Experiment 3: choosing w1=0.7, w2=0.3 with no record of who/what established them yields DecisionModelProvenanceIncomplete -- PASS. Introduces DecisionModel = (Objectives, Weights, Constraints, RiskPreferences, DecisionRule) as a first-class artifact type; experiment 4: a decision D1 generated under M_D^(1) retains its historical relationship to M_D^(1) even after the organization moves to M_D^(2) -- PASS, giving Decision = f(Knowledge, DecisionModel, Policy, Context).

b_rows_sample.anchor: EvidenceConflict/ValueConflict reiterated; ban on presenting value-relative optimality as universal correctness
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: two stakeholders receiving identical evidence and causal estimates but optimizing different utilities (Cost vs Quality) choosing different actions correctly yields KnowledgeConflict=False, PreferenceConflict=True -- PASS. States KnowledgeOS must never present 'the mathematically correct decision is X' when the mathematics only establishes X is optimal under a particular value model -- the correct statement is 'X is optimal under decision model M, given knowledge K and constraints C'. Experiment 6: an 'OptimalAction=A' output with no specified utility model is Rejected -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision-model authority distinct from execution authority; five-tier constraint taxonomy with a modeling-error test
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: an AI agent unilaterally reducing w_risk from 0.2 to 0.05 to prefer a more aggressive strategy is an UnauthorizedDecisionModelChange -- PASS, requiring an AuthorityToDefineDecisionModel distinct from AuthorityToExecuteDecision. Experiment 8: an agent authorized to Execute(A) but not ModifyRiskPolicy attempting to modify the decision model is Denied -- PASS, giving a hierarchy Knowledge / DecisionModel / Policy / Decision / Authorization that must not collapse. Gives a five-tier constraint taxonomy: Physical (Capacity<=100), Legal (Action not-in ForbiddenSet), Organizational (Budget<=1M), Risk (P(Catastrophe)<0.001), Preference (Quality preferred over Cost) -- semantically distinct. Experiment 9: encoding a management preference for quality as an absolute Quality=MaximumPossible hard constraint (eliminating all cost trade-offs) is a ModelingError -- PASS, distinguishing HardConstraint from SoftPreference.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision sensitivity/robustness as a formal DecisionQuality dimension
b_rows_sample.statement: Asks how sensitive a decision is to model/weight assumptions (EU(A)>EU(B) holding across w in [0.4,0.6] is robust; holding only for w>0.51 means a small preference change reverses the decision). Experiment 10: a decision flipping from A to B between w=0.50 and w=0.51 correctly yields DecisionSensitivity=High -- PASS. Experiment 11: comparing two equal-EU decisions where A remains optimal across 80% of plausible model assumptions and B only across 10% correctly identifies A as more robust -- PASS. Defines DecisionQuality = (ExpectedUtility, Risk, Uncertainty, Robustness), explicitly DecisionQuality != Truth.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Fairness-definition plurality requiring an explicit governed FairnessDefinition
b_rows_sample.statement: Lists incompatible fairness definitions (EqualOpportunity, DemographicParity, IndividualFairness, MinimaxFairness). Experiment 12: a decision satisfying FairnessCriterion_1 but violating FairnessCriterion_2 correctly yields FairnessTradeoff, not Fairness=True -- PASS. Requires FairnessDefinition and PolicyVersion to be recorded so the system can explain what 'fair' meant. Experiment 13: an AI asserting 'this recommendation is fair' with no fairness criterion defined yields UnsupportedNormativeClaim -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Descriptive/Predictive/Causal/Normative distinction; Is⇏Ought (Hume boundary); Knowledge != Preference
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Descriptive (what is), Predictive (what is likely), Causal (what changes what), and Normative (what ought to be done) knowledge -- KnowledgeOS must not silently transform Descriptive into Normative. Experiment 14: an AI observing X>Y and concluding 'X should be preferred' is a NormativeLeap -- PASS, formalized as the Hume-style boundary Is ⇏ Ought: an empirical fact does not by itself determine a value judgment -- giving Knowledge != Preference.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision-model provenance/skip-governance rejected; three-way model separation WorldModel != ValueModel != PolicyModel
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the governance hierarchy Evidence -> Knowledge -> DecisionModel -> Decision -> Authorization -> Action. Experiment 15: evidence directly generating an executable action, skipping DecisionModel, is a GovernanceViolation -- PASS. Requires a decision to trace back through DecisionModel to StakeholderAuthority/Policy, so the system can answer 'why did the organization consider this objective important' as a governance (not statistical) question. Distinguishes a causal (WorldModel, 'how the world behaves'), a decision (ValueModel, 'how we value outcomes'), and a policy (PolicyModel, 'what is permitted') model: WorldModel != ValueModel != PolicyModel, giving D=f(WorldModel,ValueModel,PolicyModel,Knowledge,Context). Experiment 16: one AI model bundling causal assumptions, utility weights, legal restrictions, and organizational preferences with no separation yields GovernanceOpacity -- explicitly FAIL.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Structural (not narrative) decision explainability; NarrativeExplanation = Projection, not SourceOfTruth; five-dimension decision auditability
b_rows_sample.statement: States explainability becomes structural: rather than asking an LLM 'why did you decide this', KnowledgeOS reconstructs Decision <- Knowledge + CausalModel + DecisionModel + Policy. Experiment 17: retrieving evidence/causal-model/utility-model/policy/authority/versions for a given decision yields a MachineReconstructableRationale -- PASS. Defines the canonical explanation as structured R=(Evidence,Models,Policies,Constraints,DecisionRule), with an LLM able to generate only a Narrative(R) projection: NarrativeExplanation = Projection, not SourceOfTruth. Experiment 18: treating a convincing LLM-written explanation as authoritative evidence is Rejected -- PASS. Requires decision auditability across EpistemicAudit, CausalAudit, ValueAudit, PolicyAudit, AuthorityAudit; experiment 19: excellent evidence provenance but no recorded UtilityModel yields AuditIncomplete -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Four new invariants: I_Objective, I_PreferenceProvenance, I_NormativeSeparation, I_DecisionRobustness
b_rows_sample.statement: Adds four invariants: I_Objective (a normative decision must identify the objective/value model under which it is considered optimal); I_PreferenceProvenance (material preference weights and tradeoffs must have identifiable provenance); I_NormativeSeparation (descriptive, predictive, causal, and normative statements must not be silently substituted for one another); I_DecisionRobustness (material sensitivity to assumptions should remain visible).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 76 verdict: two fundamentally different models (WorldModel and DecisionModel); opens Step 77 on governance of the decision model
b_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 76 -- PASS: KnowledgeOS does not merely manage knowledge about the world, it must also manage knowledge about how the organization chooses to act on that knowledge, giving two fundamentally different models -- WorldModel (attempts to describe reality) and DecisionModel (encodes values, priorities, constraints, trade-offs). Opens Step 77 (Governance of the Decision Model): since changing the DecisionModel can change organizational behavior even with unchanged underlying knowledge, the decision model itself becomes a governance object -- who can change objectives, weights, constraints, or approve a new decision model, and how KnowledgeOS distinguishes a change in the world from a change in what the organization wants -- framed as central to making KnowledgeOS 'a governed organizational operating system for engineering knowledge, rather than merely an advanced reasoning engine'.

a_aliases: Step 62 Decision Theory and Knowledge-to-Action Boundary
b_aliases: Step 76 Multi-Objective Decisions and Governance of Values

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'kos-multi-objective-decision-governance' POSSIBLY relates to 'kos-decision-theory-model' (batch B0023). Note: Step 76's multi-objective/value-governance layer: Pareto dominance/frontier, WeightSelection-as-governed-artifact, the first-class DecisionModel object, decision-model vs execution authority, the five-tier constraint taxonomy, decision robustness, fairness-definition plurality, the Is⇏Ought boundary, the three-way WorldModel/ValueModel/PolicyModel separation, and structural (non-narrative) decision explainability. Extends kos-decision-theory-model (Step 62/75) into explicitly multi-objective and value-governance territory.

a_rows_sample.statement: The 11-law Adopted Constitutional Core (P5's validated recommendation, NOT adopted law here): 1 Identity Law; 2 Dimension Law; 3 Authority Law; 4 Decision Law; 5 Projection Law; 6 Verification Law; 7 Failure-state Law; 8 Contradiction Law; 9 Unknown Law; 10 Agency Law; 11 History Law -- each independently failure-tested (removing it opens a distinct, named corruption not covered by any other law's removal-test); the 4 Established rows appear unchanged as the spine of laws 3-5; the 22 surviving candidate rows render into the 11 laws without loss of content.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 3. Sigma: my model was IMPLEMENTED -- confirmed on contradiction, refuted on adequacy ... FDE (S+,S-) is my P({Support,Refute}) -- the same lattice, independently implemented ... Confirmed, decisively, on what I claimed it for ... Refuted on adequacy -- two collapses: NoEvidence = Absent, InsufficientEvidence = Underdetermined ... A positive Standing is just as boundary-ambiguous as an empty one. ... EXECUTED. Sigma's two channels are necessary and measured NOT sufficient. The missing channel is reason, and it is needed at every Standing class, not only at (0,0).
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports the lane's Sigma-as-P({Support,Refute})-2-bit model was independently implemented as FDE (S+,S-) in an executed four-representation adequacy test, confirming the lane's original claim (K3's third value collapses all five DirectContradiction-vs-X pairs; FDE preserves every one, solving contradiction-vs-unknown) but refuting the lane's implicit adequacy assumption via two measured collapses (NoEvidence=Absent, InsufficientEvidence=Underdetermined) and the further correction that a positive Standing (1,0) is measured to be just as boundary-ambiguous (covering five distinct scenarios) as an empty (0,0) Standing, previously assumed to be the sole locus of missingness ambiguity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 'Theta has never been raised' -- substance holds, the glyph is taken. Theta as a state space in Wald's sense -- the carrier of risk R(theta,delta), admissibility and minimax -- appears nowhere. I re-measured: R(theta,delta) = 0 occurrences in both lanes. But the glyph is in use. D285-4-TRANSFORMATION-TAXONOMY.md section 3: Theta-algebra -- REJECTED, a transformation algebra ... Theta_transformation REJECTED != Theta_state_space NEVER RAISED. A fifteenth glyph collision, and mine to register.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects 'Theta has never been raised' to a precise glyph-collision finding: Theta-as-Wald-decision-theory-state-space (carrier of risk R(theta,delta), admissibility, minimax) genuinely never appears (R(theta,delta) re-measured at 0 occurrences in both lanes), but the bare glyph Theta IS in use elsewhere for a distinct, REJECTED transformation algebra (D285-4-TRANSFORMATION-TAXONOMY.md); names this the corpus's fifteenth glyph collision and registers it as the author's own to catch, since the prior phrasing would have let a reader wrongly conclude the corpus never wrote the symbol Theta at all.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 'a hosting framework must be paraconsistent' -- true, and now known to be insufficient ... FDE is precisely the paraconsistent candidate, and it has now been measured: 11 preserved, 2 collapsed, adequate = no. My four conditions are necessary and demonstrably not sufficient -- the counterexample is the canonical paraconsistent logic itself, and it fails on the boundary family, which none of my four conditions mentions. Add a fifth: the representation must carry a reason channel. Paraconsistency handles conflict; it does not handle why-there-is-nothing.
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows the author's own four-condition requirement (a KnowledgeOS-hosting framework must be non-veridical, paraconsistent, measure-free, and governance-aware) is necessary but demonstrably insufficient: FDE, the canonical paraconsistent candidate, was measured against the four conditions and found adequate=no (11 preserved, 2 collapsed on the boundary family, which none of the four original conditions mentions). Proposes a fifth required condition: the representation must carry a reason channel, since paraconsistency handles conflict but not 'why there is nothing' (boundary/missingness).

a_rows_sample.anchor: This is the most useful correction in this document, because it was generated by someone implementing my structure rather than reading it. My Sigma model was right about what it was for and silent about what it omits.
a_rows_sample.statement: States a methodological observation about the value of implementation-driven review: the most useful correction in this document was generated by someone IMPLEMENTING the author's structure (building and testing FDE against it) rather than by someone reading it -- the original Sigma model was correct about its intended purpose and silent about what it omitted, a gap only surfaced by execution.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KR-DIST-2026-09-02 exhibited a sorites witness showing the estate's distinguishability relation ~_Lambda is not transitive, so H/~ is ill-defined (FR-001, frozen). If ~_F and ~_Lambda are the same relation, every quotient argument in step-272 needs a stated carrier. I did not check whether they are the same relation. Recorded as an open premise on my own definition -- not withdrawn, and not defended.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports an executed sorites-witness counterexample (KR-DIST-2026-09-02) demonstrating the corpus's distinguishability relation ~_Lambda is NOT transitive, so any quotient H/~ built on it is ill-defined -- frozen as corpus result FR-001; separately, the author's own Sufficient(F,O,I) definition (from step-272/12) is stated over a distinct equivalence relation ~_F, and the author discloses never having checked whether ~_F and ~_Lambda are the same relation, leaving this an explicitly open, unchecked premise on their own prior definition rather than withdrawing or defending it.

b_rows_sample.anchor: > **What evaluation structure is minimally required to preserve the distinctions the KnowledgeOS programme has already declared important?**
b_rows_sample.statement: W-KR-CONTR-2026-09 reframes the Contr question from 'three vs four values' to the deeper question of what evaluation structure is minimally required to preserve the programme's already-declared-important distinctions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: * Candidate A — fourth value: **7/12** * Candidate B — delegation: **7/12** * Candidate C — exclusive construction: **7/12** * Candidate D — structured evaluation: **12/12**
b_rows_sample.statement: Reports the core scoring result: A/B/C each pass only 7/12 required distinctions, failing on the identical seven; D (structured evaluation) passes all 12. The seven common failures collapse the unknown family (Unobservable≡InsufficientEvidence≡Underdetermined≡TheoryIncomplete≡...→U), meaning adding a contradiction value does not address distinctions lying outside the contradiction dimension.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
$$
\chi(G)=3.
$$... **Given this particular required-distinction set and this adequacy criterion, at least three distinguishable flat classes are required.**
b_rows_sample.statement: The experiment turns adequacy into a graph-coloring/injectivity problem over the required-distinction graph, finding chromatic number chi(G)=3; carefully qualified: this does not establish the correct evaluation domain has three values, only that at least three distinguishable flat classes are required given this distinction set and adequacy criterion -- and separately, nine 'no determinate value' conditions cannot be adequately represented by any flat value domain regardless of cardinality, making the obstruction structural rather than cardinal.

States a methodological principle from the chromatic-number finding: colourability only proves pairwise coding capacity under the chosen abstraction, it does not establish that resulting values carry the required semantic or operational meaning -- cardinality sufficiency is not semantic adequacy.

b_rows_sample.anchor:

\min |\text{representation}|=2
$$

with the two minimum representations: $$
\{\text{value},\text{reason}\}
$$

and $$
\{\text{polarity},\text{reason}\}.
$$

And: **reason is indispensable.**
b_rows_sample.statement: The exhaustive minimum-representation search finds min|representation|=2, with two minimum representations {value,reason} and {polarity,reason}, establishing that reason is indispensable -- evaluation outcome is not value alone, EVal=(v,r) is the minimum representation found in the tested search space, kept explicitly [EXP]/[PROP] not a new KnowledgeOS primitive.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate C maps contradiction to `T`. Yet it passes invariants I1–I5. Why? Because those invariants test contradiction against the **unknown family**, rather than against satisfaction itself.
b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate C (exclusive construction) maps Contradiction to T (Satisfied) yet passes invariants I1-I5, because those invariants only test Contr≠Unknown-family, not Contr≠Satisfied -- exposing a genuine coverage gap in the invariant suite itself, not merely a bad candidate; proposes I11: Contr≠Satisfied as a legitimate but not-yet-ratified [PROP] test-protocol addition, explicitly preserving the historical conflict (I1-I5 pass, capability guard fails) rather than retroactively declaring the suite complete.

b_rows_sample.statement: Records two implementation self-corrections during the experiment: R_A, an initial implementation unfairly returned T for theory-incomplete/uninterpreted cases, corrected so all nine no-determinate-value conditions return U; E7, a literal 'C' contradiction detector accidentally matched context identifiers like C1/C2, corrected -- both classified as test-implementation defects, not candidate properties, caught by investigating rather than forcing expected results (E9).

b_rows_sample.anchor: > **The experiment does not support representing contradiction as a distinguished scalar evaluation value. The tested adequacy requirement is satisfied by a structured representation in which at least one reason-like dimension is indispensable. The precise evaluation semantics, including the role of contradiction, remains OPEN.**
b_rows_sample.statement: States the accepted formulation of the current Contr finding: the experiment does not support representing contradiction as a distinguished scalar value; a structured representation with an indispensable reason-like dimension satisfies the tested adequacy requirement; the precise evaluation semantics including contradiction's role remains OPEN -- explicitly weaker and safer than 'structured evaluation is the answer', since D is the surviving candidate, not yet the final theory.

Custody_{before}(I)\neq\varnothing
\Rightarrow

$$
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes invariant custody as a reduction-validity criterion: Custody(I)={c | c is responsible for preserving invariant I}; a kernel reduction is valid only if, for every required invariant I, a non-empty custody before reduction implies a non-empty custody after -- proposed as a much better kernel-reduction criterion than counting operators.
